Collisions between atomic nuclei generate significant fluctuations in baryon (or quark) number density. These density variations are deeply connected to local properties of the quark--gluon plasma (QGP), such as the speed of sound and critical points. We propose a novel approach to constrain these variables and initial conditions by examining the spectral density of fluctuations in the Higgs field at the LHC. Specifically, we show that two-particle correlation at non-zero transverse momentum serves as a sensitive probe of initial baryon number density fluctuations. Our estimates of these correlations near the critical point suggest that Higgs fluctuation measurements could be achieved with current data taken by the ATLAS and ALICE experiments at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV. This methodology provides a direct probe of initial conditions and the specific heat close to the critical point, utilizing well-established analysis techniques and existing data. Consequently, future experiments can more precisely determine the location and characteristics of the critical point by targeting the region of minimum the slope of the specific heat versus temperature curve.

While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to incorporate additional constraints regarding the presence or absence of nulls. We characterize this problem by defining a minimal, canonical, and normal form for the set of functional dependencies encompassing such constraints; a instance satisfies the table's conditions if and only if it meets all associated functional dependencies. AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, we apply the TV-PARX model to real-world count data, comparing its results against those of other time-varying models and established nonlinear frameworks, including Poisson and Exponential Linear Models. Empirical findings indicate that TV-PARX delivers superior in-sample fits and more accurate out-of-sample forecasts compared to its counterparts. Additionally, the model's capability to estimate time-varying parameters is highlighted through the analysis of specific economic phenomena, such as holiday effects in sales data and the impact of technology adoption on carbon emissions. Finally, we provide a user-friendly guide to facilitate the practical implementation of the TV-PARX model. The accompanying R source code is available at http://sites.unmonde.com/gparx/. 
Keywords: Count time series, Time-varying parameters, Poisson distribution, PARX model, Score-driven processes, Holiday effects, Technology adoption.

Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. Multi-object tracking (MOT) is essential for assigning identities to detected objects across video frames, yet achieving this in unstructured environments remains difficult due to challenges in generalizing detections across different object instances and occlusions. While recent methods attempt to solve this by learning a global 3D descriptor for each detected instance, these approaches often require extensive supervision, including difficult negative samples and multi-object trajectories. In this paper, we propose a multi-stage approach to build and maintain short-term 3D embeddings that are robust to camera pose and specific to each instance. Our method jointly exploits the translation equivariance of phase codes in SIamese StereoSOFTMAX networks and the rotational equivariance of local feature aggregations in a graph-based module. This allows us to generalize instance IDs beyond overlapping detection ranges and occlusions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our instance-specific 3D descriptor in a new, fully supervised MOT algorithm. Experiments on two real-world datasets, MOT17 and UAV123, show that our 3D instance embeddings are highly generalizable and facilitate accurate ID tracking up to 20 meters of translation and 3 Hz in frequency. Source code is available at https://github.com/Byt3n3ss/MOT-NDF.

Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. This paper focuses on refining the postprocessing stage of a two-stage pipeline by integrating projection grouping and correspondence learning to estimate poses in challenging scenarios. First, a local patch-based method predicts projection heatmaps representing the confidence distribution of 3D bounding box corners. A proposed projection grouping module then eliminates redundant local maxima across heatmap layers. Rather than directly applying the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm to 2D-3D correspondences, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, and a correspondence selector leverages pairwise relationships to identify the most probable set. Experiments across three public datasets show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art correspondence-selection-based techniques and existing direct regression methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengnien/Projection-Based-PoseEstimation .

to address General Graphical Lasso problems. Building on the Graphical Lasso method introduced by Friedman et al. (2007), our work extends this framework to accommodate broader estimation scenarios. Specifically, we generalize the approach to handle node subsets and conditional sets of covariates or responses, covering cases where some variables are missing at random or missing completely at random. To ensure robustness, the package includes multiple hypothesis testing procedures to control the false discovery rate. The software is optimized for efficiency and scalability, capable processing networks with millions of edges on standard hardware. We demonstrate its utility through a wide range of applications, including estimating a global stock market network via a multivariate BEKK model and analyzing multivariate GARCH models across global financial institutions. The GGLasso library implements several state-of-the-art algorithms, including a highly efficient higher-order proximal message passing method (HoPMP) and a fast parallel operator splitting method (FPOM). Our benchmarks show that HoPMP outperforms existing solutions for sparse graphical models with conditional responses or exogenous covariates, while FPOM serves as a robust fallback option. Furthermore, our results indicate that assuming specific data structures, even when invalid, can lead to inefficient or unusable estimates. The library is released under an open-access license, and the source code is available at https://github.com/andrewggl/GGLasso.

Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. of eigenvector centrality within multilayer networks that incorporate inter-layer constraints on node significance. This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to be derived from any layer of the multilayer system. Furthermore, the system incorporates constraints that cap a node's potential importance in one layer based on its actual importance in a different layer. The objective is to determine the equilibrium state of the network, accounting for these dynamic constraints alongside the shared node set. To achieve this, we formulate and resolve multiple systems of nonlinear equations utilizing continuation methods, ensuring the solutions adhere to the imposed inter-layer constraints. The final output provides a comprehensive assessment of node importance across all layers. We validate this approach through both a numerical example and an application to a DNA gene regulation multilayer network, demonstrating that the resulting layer-specific importance scores align with established biological findings. Additionally, we show that our method generalizes and offers advantages over existing techniques designed for simpler multilayer network variants. Key contributions include: (a) defining a straightforward yet powerful framework for evaluating node importance in multilayer networks with constrained inter-layer dynamics, applicable to various scientific domains; (b) developing efficient numerical algorithms to compute equilibrium states and derive a capped eigenvector centrality matrix matrix $M^{capped}_A(x)$. These findings enable the characterization of all local minima and the efficient determination of initial states converging to them via forward iteration. Crucially, this framework is applicable to directed multilayer networks featuring both weighted edges and multiple constrained layers sharing identical node sets. We illustrate the method's utility with a numerical example and a DNA gene regulation case study, highlighting how assigned importance propagates across layers due to imposed constraints, even when no direct edges exist between layers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this technique efficiently resolves the challenge of calculating the most probable hidden state sequence for a given observed state in Markov Hidden Status Fields networks. Finally, we establish that the algorithm effectively calculates the Viterbi path in Markov Hidden Status Field networks. In summary, this work presents an efficient algorithm for finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) hidden state sequence in

In this paper, we derive the Dirac equation within $R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish its equivalence to the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime expressed via its conformally flat metric. This phenomenon distinguishes between low-speed ($U<25$~m/s) and high-speed ($U>100$$-$200~m/s) conditions based on the Weber number $We=\rho UD/\sigma$. By examining extensive families of four-dimensional Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify potential generalized global symmetries and demonstrate how they are circumvented. A key component in these theories involves generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear interactions between axion fields and gauge field strength terms quadratic in topology, thereby disrupting a significant portion of global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can break any remaining residual symmetries. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinitely populated lattice. We also demonstrate that this lattice arises from the monodromy transformation acting on the moduli space boundary where the effective theory is defined. Ultimately, we establish that this lattice corresponds to the extended gauge symmetry of an enhanced gauge symmetry point in the moduli space bulk. Additionally, we provide a mapping between the boundary conditions of generic $\theta$-terms and the enhancement of the $SO(8)$ symmetry of the heterotic string compactified on $T^6$. Finally, we offer suggestions regarding the breakdown of generalized $\theta$-terms and the associated charged state spectrum when a generalized T-duality is applied. Our primary objective in this study is to illustrate, through concrete examples, how charged states can disrupt generalized global symmetries, thereby allowing the theory to evade the no-global symmetry theorem and maintain its consistency. Along the way, we uncover a novel mechanism by which charged states can form an infinitely populated lattice, distinct from the standard wall-crossing phenomena observed in other $\mathcal{N}=2$ theories.

This uncommon configuration in $3d$ transition metal compounds provides an explanation for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous M\"ossbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic ordering between nearest-neighbor Fe ions. Using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding model with horizontal and vertical hopping, we identify two non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry trajectory. These cones can be manipulated through various Hamiltonian perturbations that break lattice symmetries; initially, we introduce distinct onsite potentials, which cause the Dirac cones to evolve into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along high-symmetry paths. Subsequently, we apply hopping term dimerization, observing the migration of Dirac cones along the first Brillouin zone trajectory, followed by their annihilation and reappearance from a semi-Dirac cone state. Finally, we elaborate further details regarding the spectrum and band structure along several chosen paths. This final segment also encompasses the impact of symmetry breaking along the BZ trajectory when the lattice undergoes spatial dimerization, resulting in a Mott-insulator phase. Throughout the study, the opening and closing of energy gaps, along with the displacement and disappearance of Dirac cones, are highlighted. The findings presented herein may assist in investigating symmetry-breaking phenomena within symmetry-adapted non-symmorphic electronic lattices. Specifically, the transitions between Dirac cones, semi-Dirac cones, and energy gaps could indicate topological phase transitions, potentially leading to Majorana fermions or other exotic particles. Additionally, the lattice symmetry breaking detailed in this work resembles the "crayfish track" pattern observed in the honeycomb lattice under external electric fields, a phenomenon linked to the quantum Hall effect and the generation of chiral edge states. Consequently, the symmetry breaking effects explored in this paper could be harnessed to generate similar "crayfish track" patterns, potentially enabling the formation of quantum defects or edge states useful in the design of topological electronic devices. Alongside these applications, the "crayfish track" pattern is also significant in biological and medical fields for detecting diseases such as cancer and various pathogens. Ultimately, the detailed behaviors of the energy spectrum and band structure along the first Brillouin zone, along with the associated wavefunctions and their probability densities across the lattice, may prove valuable in actual semiconductor lattice implementations. This is because the described symmetry-breaking mechanisms can be utilized to create Schottky diodes and other electronic components based on crayfish-track semiconducting defects on graphene-based herringbone lattices.

These states emerge from one output port of the BS or PA when a coherent state and a single-photon Fock state occupy the two input ports, provided a single photon is detected in the remaining output port. Quantum states of light are increasingly being utilized to represent and manipulate quantum bits and dits in computation and communication tasks. Among the diverse range of states, optical catalyzed states have garnered significant attention due to their abundant nonclassical features. These states are constructed by conditionally applying a measurement on a catalytic resource to a target state within the framework of quantum optics. First introduced by Aharonov and Popescu in 1993 as "absorbing states," this concept was later renamed to "quantum-optical catalyzed states." Additionally, quantum-optical catalyzed states were documented by Sreekanth and Joshi in 2020 using a parabolic potential. This review aims to present the fundamental concepts and computational procedures regarding these bivectors, specifically by transforming the complex self-dual electromagnetic field from an orthonormal Minkowski basis into a complex null tetrad basis. Additionally, within this framework, the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the Newman-Penrose formalism are derived. This study introduces a computational approach leveraging artificial intelligence to automatically detect and segment esophageal tumors using only CT images. We collected data from 30 patients with esophageal cancer and trained a fully convolutional neural network (FCNN) to predict tumor masks. To address anatomical variability, our model incorporates random patient-specific features, including gender, left-right coordinate normalization, and the positioning of adjacent organs like the heart and liver. To mitigate the limited dataset size, we developed a data augmentation technique that synthetically adds tumor masks to healthy esophageal volumes by combining patient-specific features and random noise, trained via an end-to-end adagrad network. Evaluations on a test set and a separate clinical study demonstrated that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches without utilizing any auxiliary information. Furthermore, our solution exhibits robustness against anatomical variations and can be enhanced by integrating supplementary data when available. Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies for low-resource languages often rely on code-mixed or multilingual data, which can introduce complexities and difficulties. This document explores code-mixing phenomena related to sentiment analysis in a Bengali-English context. We establish that for NLP tasks involving low-resource languages, meticulous data preprocessing is essential. By examining the impact of various preprocessing techniques, we demonstrate that morphosyntactic features significantly enhance task performance. The proposed Bengali morphosyntactic preprocessing method is applicable to other downstream NLP tasks such as machine translation, text classification, and other NLT challenges associated with low-resource languages. Our dataset supports research on single-task NLP problems in the Bengali-English mixing environment. The findings from this study on code-mixing are relevant to any NLP task where low-resource and high-resource languages are combined. The dataset and statistics are accessible at http://nlp4sd.org/bangla-msd/ and at https://drive.google.com/file/d/1y7y05000000000000000

I contend that more detailed guidelines are necessary, ones that balance the specific requirements of visually impaired users with the practical feasibility of generating appropriate descriptions. To develop a high-quality dataset, we can leverage recent advances in machine translation, treating image description generation as a translation task where the image serves as the source and English text as the target, utilizing high-quality bilingual datasets. This study presents a novel framework combining diversity-based and relevance-based evaluation methods. For relevance, we adapt an existing model trained on high-quality multilingual datasets to estimate semantic similarity between an automatic description and a foreign-language reference. For diversity, we trained models exclusively on a single-language dataset and assessed their performance against a diversity-based metric using a foreign-language description dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address the limitations of current automatic description evaluation by integrating both relevance and diversity metrics. The proposed framework was tested on existing English and French datasets, yielding results that align well with human evaluations. Furthermore, we developed a new, higher-quality English description dataset by adapting translation models from an English-French bilingual dataset; like the French dataset, it includes diverse references ranging from short phrases to long, detailed sentences. This research investigates whether location matters by analyzing the dissemination of false COVID-19 health information—specifically the claim that the virus can be cured by drinking bleach—across U.S. counties. We identify the level of political polarization within each county, measure the distance between counties, and construct a graph where nodes represent counties and edge weights correspond to the strength of political relatedness. Our temporal analysis reveals three distinct phases of misinformation spread that align with clusters of politically similar counties, with evidence of counter-cascades and localized peaks of misinformation intensity. Furthermore, we compare political vs. geographic proximity using regression discontinuity designs; these results indicate that geographic proximity alone accounts for approximately 50 percent of the clustering observed when considering only direct geographic neighbors, suggesting that the spatial diffusion of this misinformation is heavily influenced by political homophily. Finally, we discuss the policy implications of this finding. This work utilizes a novel dataset comprising nearly real-time estimates of political polarization derived from changes in Senate voting correlations. Counterfactual experiments further support the conclusion that political homophily drives geographic diffusion. Prior to the outbreak of this misinformation, counties with lower levels of political clustering demonstrated a significantly reduced tendency to adopt behavioral patterns from neighboring counties that had been exposed to the misinformation. Recent evidence indicates that geographic clustering of misinformation correlates with higher levels of falsehoods regarding COVID-19 health guidelines and lower vaccination rates. Although demonstrations offer a natural method for teaching robots, relying solely on movement trajectories fails to incorporate other modalities, such as audio cues from human instructors. To harness these audio signals effectively, it is essential to first identify the specific information they convey. This study characterizes the audio generated by human teachers performing multi-step manipulation tasks for a Sawyer robot by analyzing three feature categories: speech duration, prosodic expressiveness, and semantic content. Although conformal field theories (CFTs) are powerful frameworks for investigating statistical field systems and their associated complexities, fully exploiting their potential requires incorporating fields into the calculation—a process that obstructs deriving general conclusions. Furthermore, while CFTs offer an holographic dual description via complex gravity models, the utility of this approach is limited by the difficulty of solving these models for intricate configurations. This study introduces a novel method to compute complexity for certain states in three-dimensional (2+1 dimensional) CFTs featuring an additional Z₂ symmetry. By leveraging the dual gravitational description, we evaluate complexity for this Z₂-symmetry-breaking state in both Euclidean and Lorentzian zones. Our findings indicate that, contrary to the situation in the Euclidean zone, complexity grows linearly with time in the Lorentzian regime for states characterized by Z₂ symmetry breaking. Additionally, we observe that incorporating charge into the gravitational model alters the time evolution of complexity. These results extend directly to Z₂-symmetric CFTs supporting global U(1) symmetries, including the Potts model and various spin models, as well as their holographic counterparts. Finally, we suggest potential applications of this approach for exploring symmetry breaking phenomena and other topics within both field-theoretic and gravitational domains.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently achieved breakthrough performance across various downstream tasks by effectively fusing multimodal data. However, current research predominantly utilizes MLLMs for single-domain tasks, failing to leverage data from related domains. This limitation restricts the model's capacity to capture comprehensive information and hinders performance, particularly in cold-start conditions. To address these challenges, we introduce a cross-domain recommendation framework designed for movie recommendation that simultaneously exploits movie graph data from related domains. This approach enhances the source domain by integrating complementary data while preserving the target domain's distribution. Our method incorporates three key innovations: (1) a hetero-enhanced graph cross attention network for capturing complementary information, (2 a triple fusion aggregation network for preserving domain specificity, and (3) adaptive domain selection to reduce parameter overhead and mitigate cold-start issues. Experimental results across three datasets confirm that our proposed framework significantly outperforms baseline methods. Additionally, our findings offer practical insights for optimizing the pretraining of multimodal large language models. Additonal analysis and visualizations are available at: https://zhangzeyu1002.github.io/CDMLLM/. Additonal code is available at: https://github.com/ZeyuZhang1002/CDMLLM.

However, these extended forms are frequently far larger and more intricate than equivalent conic natural formulations, which can leverage a wider variety of "exotic" cones. We classify exotic cones based on their ability to model specific convex cones of interest—such as the geometric program (GP) power mean cone within the positive semidefinite cone (PSD), or the entropy cone within the positive definite cone—as well as their computational viability, defined by the polynomial-time solvability of the associated conic linear system ax+b>=0 for a given vector x. This categorization yields a framework for constructing valid exotic cones capable of representing various GP power mean cones. Building on this, we propose an innovative approach to solve the convex natural formulation of the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) problem for Gaussian graphical models via its equivalent GP natural formulation. Our method involves identifying exotic cones that efficiently represent the necessary GP extended formulations for specific graph structures. By integrating these findings, we develop a novel algorithm for MLE in Gaussian graphical models. Computational results demonstrate that, unlike existing methods, our algorithm remains effective for sparse graphs containing positive correlation cycles, achieving state-of-the-art performance on several well-known sparse graphs. We attribute this success to the deliberate and strategic use of exotic cones. To support this, we provide an open-source implementation of a solver for convex optimization problems involving exotic cones, named CONEX. We hope this work encourages researchers to explore various exotic cones when addressing problems within their domain. (CONEX is accessible at: https://github.com/soheila/CONEX).

Although various advanced methods now exist for automated MRI preprocessing, the specific requirements for large studies often necessitate adapting these pipelines. This paper details an end-to-end QC pipeline developed for the discovery phase of the UK BiBank MRI project, a large-scale longitudinal investigation into brain development and aging. The approach begins with a specialized preprocessing pipeline ensuring pipeline-wide quality through automated error handling and error-aware preprocessing settings. Building on this foundation, the method integrates pipeline-wide and feature-level quality assessments, combining derived metadata (such as header information and image statistics) with deep learning-based image quality estimators. The pipeline utilizes a modular design, allowing for the inclusion of various metadata sources and metadata learning approaches, culminating in a comprehensive quality score. The UK BiBank MRI project aims to process approximately 14,000 T1-weighted MRI scans (around 300 MB each) from roughly 25,000 individuals annually; the described pipeline is designed to reduce this data volume by an order of magnitude (to ~1,400 MRIs per subject) by filtering out images with MRI artifacts, header inconsistencies, biological contaminants (like hair, teeth, and noise), and outliers based on image statistics. The paper outlines the pipeline's development process, provides visual examples of rejected MRIs, and reports findings on rejection rates across the UK population. The presented pipeline and insights are applicable to any large-scale longitudinal study, and the code is accessible at https://github.com/BrainAgeing/UKBiBank-MRI-QC-Pipeline. The pipeline was last updated on October 18, 2021.

Furthermore, we calculated the magnetic phase diagram based on the Heisenberg model for both RS and LC3 structures, revealing that the RS structure possesses lower total energy and higher total magnetic moment compared to the LC3 structure. an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. The anticipated new physics consists of gauge bosons and three replicas of a nonet consisting of scalar and vector bileptons. Assuming that the third family originates from dark matter, implying that the heaviest gauge bosons and bileptons are excluded from the visible universe, the framework's parameter space is significantly restricted. Consequently, the analysis concentrates on the lighter sector, examining constraints imposed by dark matter density, the non-observation of narrow resonances up to several TeV in $pp$ collisions at the LHC, and data from neutrino experiments. Although the third family constitutes a substantial portion of the matter density in our universe, the remaining two families account for very little. This scenario offers a compelling indication that the third family likely stems from the dark sector. Furthermore, this approach provides an attractive mechanism for generating fermion mass hierarchies through non-sequential family embedding, as the masses of the first two families are determined by the dark matter scale associated with the third family, whereas the third family's mass scale is intrinsically linked to the dark sector. Finally, the model remains largely unconstrained, suggesting that an extended universe containing two types of matter could plausibly exist, with the third family residing within the dark sector while the first two constitute visible matter. An analogous argument can be constructed for a model featuring two dark sectors and three families.

An OGS is defined by the property that every group element can be uniquely expressed as a product of specific generator powers in a fixed sequence. Regarding symmetric groups $S_n$, R. Shwartz has shown a significant link between OGS and the standard Coxeter presentation of $S_n$, termed the standard OGS of $S_n$. This paper extends that standard OGS to the finite classical Coxeter group $B_n$. We detail the exchange laws for this generalized standard OGS of $B_n$ and establish its relationship with the Coxeter length and descent set of $B_n$. Furthermore, we provide an explicit algorithm to determine whether two elements are equivalent under the standard OGS of $B_n$, confirming its validity. Finally, we examine the 8x8 Sudoku matrix group and demonstrate that the standard OGS of $B_4$ serves as its basis. Our findings are presented in four sections: Section 1 covers the definition and fundamental properties of the standard OGS of $B_n$; Section 2 offers an algorithm to verify if two elements are equivalent under this system; Section 3 investigates the correspondence between the standard OGS of $B_n$ and the Coxeter length and descent set; and Section 4 presents results on the Sudoku matrix group utilizing the standard OGS of $B_n$. The box cross change operation, a key move in solving Sudoku puzzles, is derived from the standard OGS of $B_4$. Our principal contributions lie in Sections 2, 3, and 4. Standard OGS was first introduced by R. Shwartz for $S_n$ in his 2019 work. Additionally, we determine the group order for the Sudoku matrix group using the standard OGS of $B_4$, a result that aligns with previous determinations found in the literature.

This estimator, called LensingFromIa (LFI), functions as a null test for assumptions regarding the smoothness and homogeneity of the universe. Specifically, LFI infers the mass-to-light ratio within the probed redshift and radius ranges as $f_\star = -0.204^{+0.224}_{-0.264} \pm 0.105 (E_z) \pm 0.010 (R)$, a result consistent with expectations for dark energy and supernova populations when analyzed individually. The total uncertainty comprises statistical error (0.010), simulation noise (0.105), sample covariance between Type Ia supernovae and weak lensing (0.143), and uncertainties linked to $w_0$ and $w_a$ (0.143). With current datasets, the per-redshift accuracy for E(z) and the per-angular-size accuracy for R are approximately 3% and 7%, respectively. Although the present UPTF1111 dataset yields no significant constraints on $w_0$ and $w_a$, our forecasts indicate that adding LFI to UPTF and SDSS data could constrain $|w_0|$ to 0.10 and $|w_a|$ to 0.20. We outline the necessary conditions for achieving these precision goals, emphasizing the need to mitigate sample covariance and construct a deeper, wider SDSS supernova catalog. The LFI method is readily applicable to existing datasets and will soon be implemented with new surveys such as LSST and DESI. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to some claims, the evolution of $w$ is not inherently difficult to constrain with future data, and the primary obstacle to precision is sample covariance rather than angular diameter distance. Furthermore, we provide code for implementing LFI and define the improvements required to achieve the forecasted gains. We argue that incorporating lensing information from Type Ia supernovae is crucial for fully exploiting the potential of upcoming surveys to constrain dark energy properties.

Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into context-dependent groups: (1) Single Image Detectors (SIDs), (2) Multi Image Detectors (MIDs), (3) Multi Object Detectors (MODs), and (2) Task Auxiliary Detectors (TADs). We evaluate each category's utilization of context through ablation studies and demonstrate that higher-level context does not always enhance performance. Consequently, we offer targeted recommendations context-aware users can apply to fine-tune detectors for specific scenarios. Notably, for single-shot configurations with identical hyperparameters, DODs can match or surpass the COAP baseline's per-class AP by approximately 5–10 IPs. Additionally, we present a novel finding: changing the image resolution by 50% causes up to a 20% drop in AP across all detectors. Finally, we introduce a new method for estimating context budget distribution, revealing that modern detectors implicitly focus roughly 75% of their context on adjacent regions and 12.5% on background. Determining the optimal context composition remains an open challenge for future research. Our code, tables, and plots are publicly available at https://sites.google.com/view/contextdet/. Our findings contextualize current object detection capabilities and constraints, identifying key areas where future detectors can better harness context. Public resources facilitate easier exploration of context usage in state-of-the-art detectors. Our insights benefit applications with favorable context conditions, such as traffic monitoring, crowd analysis, and social media image tagging.

In a complementary paper, we introduce a complementary sieve method to address a long-standing conjecture by Kesten and Nelson: if a function on the cube is positive-definite and depends solely on an even number of variables, then it is log-concave. We further generalize this result to a broader class of positive-definite functions. Building upon these findings, we obtain improved Bernstein inequalities for such functions. Our approach relies on characterizing positive-definite functions via the spectral measure of the Dirichlet form associated with the Laplacian, utilizing a sieve technique to estimate the density of this measure. This conjecture was previously established independently by H\"ast\"o.

Concentration inequalities for matrix-valued functions on Gaussian and discrete cube domains have been explored by various authors. However, extending scalar inequalities to the matrix setting often presents challenges, as many standard transformations, such as taking norms, fail to preserve the Gaussian nature of random vectors. This document investigates similar issues within the framework of subgaussian matrix-valued functions on the discrete cube. We define a novel metric to quantify the subgaussian property and explore its fundamental properties. Our findings include equivalent conditions for matrix and singular value subgaussianity, along with relationships to standard definitions. These results lead to refined bounds for singular value subgaussian functions, generalizing inequalities by Benaych-Georges and Gu, as well as a new inequality for singular values in random projections. However, incompatible transplants carry higher risks of rejection, infection, cancer, and graft loss compared to compatible ones. This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. To model the impact of incompatibility, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework that treats compatibility as an explicit state variable. Although this results in a higher-dimensional model that complicates analysis, we derive structural properties—specifically control limit-type optimal policies—that are straightforward to calculate and apply. Numerical simulations demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves across varying mismatch levels and underscore the necessity of integrating incompatibility status directly into acceptance decisions, particularly when desensitization therapy is available. Although these findings assume first-come-first-served allocation, the core insight remains relevant for other protocols. Ultimately, our results offer actionable guidance for policymakers and clinicians regarding kidney acceptance policies that account for incompatibility and desensitization therapy, and we provide R code to calculate the resulting decision thresholds. Keywords: End-Stage Kidney Disease, Kidney Transplantation, Incompatible Kidneys, Desensitization Therapy, Optimal Stopping, Markov Decision Processes, Control Limits, Base Excess. Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) with sample complexities that are polynomial in every problem parameter, including the number of players. To accomplish this, we also propose a new, efficient method for identifying a single rationalizable action profile (which need not be an equilibrium), significantly improving upon the sample complexity achieved by Wu et al. (2021). Our approach integrates several innovative techniques to ensure both rationalizability and no (swap-)regret, such as a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which may hold independent value. We further validate our findings with a sample complexity lower bound that demonstrates the tightness of our guarantees. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence suggesting our methods are practical, as they outperform state-of-the-art single-equilibrium learning algorithms in scenarios involving many irrational players.

Rationalizable strategies constitute a rationality concept stricter than those defining equilibrium (Shoham & Leyton-Brown, 2008). A strategy is rationalizable if it is a best response to some belief about opponents' play, and this property holds recursively (Bernheim, 1984; Gibbons, 1991; Peleg & Samet, 1987). Because a action profile is rationalizable only if each action is rationalizable, a Nash Equilibrium exists among rationalizable actions (Gibbons, 1991). Beyond establishing the existence of equilibria, assessing whether played actions are rationalizable offers a more granular analysis of opponent behavior. For instance, in two-player zero-sum games, we can efficiently learn the value of the game and a Nash Equilibrium using modern sample-efficient algorithms (Audiffred et al., 2019; Gasparini et al., 2021; Karn & Shwartz-Zweir, 2020; Perdomo et al., 2020; Stankeviciute et al., 2020; Syrgiamis et al0; Syrgiamis et al., 2021; Syrgiamis et al., 2

The model's parameters are estimated using maximum likelihood estimation based on discrete-time observations of infectious individuals. While previous research derived closed-form expressions for these estimates, those formulas were developed under simplifying assumptions regarding infectious period durations that do not align with current empirical evidence. This paper introduces novel closed-form expressions for both the susceptible fraction and the mean infectious period. While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. This adaptive mechanism assigns greater weight to historical data more likely to originate from the current target distribution. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that VRER accelerates policy convergence and boosts performance across several standard environments. We introduce the MultiTalk Dataset, a collection exceeding 200,000 written dialogue sentences that achieves a balance between a high branching factor (10) and multiple conversation turns (6) via constraints on context relevance and linguistic diversity. We also offer a variety of analysis tools tailored to this branching structure, addressing both context selection issues—such as classification, similarity, and translation—as well as generation problems across single and multiple turn contexts. Furthermore, we conducted several comparative studies on models ranging from basic recurrent neural networks to complex systems utilizing social attention mechanisms across these tasks. A key finding from our work is the observation of a performance plateau in prediction accuracy, likely indicating a limit imposed by insufficient data point quality rather than a fundamental barrier to prediction. Additionally, we analyzed prediction performance in relation to context descriptiveness and discovered a surprising result: performance does not consistently improve as context descriptiveness decreases. This contradicts the common assumption that more ambiguous contexts yield more varied responses; instead, we found that ambiguity often leads to converged performance across different prediction tasks. Finally, we discussed the implications of our findings for designing artificial conversational agents. The written format of the MultiTalk Dataset, combined with its high branching factor and multi-turn nature, makes it particularly suitable for evaluating state-of-the-art predictive models in conversational contexts that more closely resemble free conversations than current standard datasets. Consequently, we suggest future research directions, including multi-turn prediction tasks, prioritization of written over spoken language in research, the exploration of the link between context descriptiveness and performance across diverse domains, and the modeling of the probability distribution of multiple correct responses. The written modality allows for comprehensive performance analyses and theoretical explorations of the relationships between branching factor, context descriptiveness, and performance—topics that remain unexamined in prior literature on spoken dialogue. The multi-turn structure of our dataset enables a detailed analysis of how the proportion of recent context impacts performance, revealing a slower decay rate in written compared to spoken dialogue. Overall, the combination of the MultiTalk Dataset and our analysis provides a robust foundation for advancing the prediction of written dialogue. The written modality is particularly advantageous for quantitative theoretical analyses of the connections between performance, branching factor, and context descriptiveness, as well as for studying the quality of responses across multiple branches. These insights are essential for developing a theoretical framework for predicting written dialogue and designing artificial conversationalists. In this work, we construct GFF-valued processes on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ and the first orthant $\mathbb{O}$ by coupling a GFF with a time-evolving multiple SLE on each domain. If this interaction violates lepton number, the $\Delta L=2$ transition is directly mediated by the dark matter field, bypassing the suppression typically caused by small neutrino masses, thereby producing a significant effect on decay rates. Because ultralight dark matter behaves as a classical field, the resulting decay events exhibit a periodic modulation. However, we observe that in the early Universe, such a coupling would likely disrupt standard cosmological models. Specifically, the necessity for neutrinos to free-stream prior to matter-radiation equality imposes strict constraints on the parameter space, rendering the detection of any signal in future $0\nu \beta\beta$ experiments extremely unlikely, even with meV-level sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass. To achieve detectability, the dark matter interaction with neutrinos must be purely dispersive; in this specific scenario, we note that decay rates scale quadratically with neutrino mass and that the lack of gradient or time derivatives in the interaction Lagrangian prevents conflicts with cosmological observations. We illustrate these dynamics using specific examples and provide analytical estimates for the key decay rate and event rate formulas.

, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, when applying NLG to model galactic rotation curves under the assumption that its constitutive relation is time-reversal invariant, the resulting galactic acceleration differs from predictions based on the electrodynamics analogy. Specifically, these curves either do not exhibit the observed flatness or require a dark matter halo. However, if time-reversal invariance is abandoned, the produced curves are nearly identical to the Einsteinian Newtonian case and remain close to those predicted by the electrodynamics analogy. In this scenario, the rotation curves are again not truly flat, and the inhomogeneity of the constitutive relation causes the required acceleration to exceed the Einstein-Newtonian value. Consequently, time-reversal invariant nonlocal gravity fails to explain galactic rotation curves, and neither the recent recent constitutive relation nor the electrodynamics analogy successfully account for this phenomenon. These findings contrast with previous studies claiming that NLG can explain galactic rotation without dark matter [28, 29, 30, 31]. Additionally, this research challenges recent claims [32] suggesting that a specific constitutive relation can explain galactic rotation curves within general relativity. Keywords: Nonlocal gravity; nonlocal electrodynamics; de Sitter spacetime; galactic rotation; dark matter. PACS: 04.20.Fy, 98.85.Kc.

We present a statistical framework that leverages genome-wide association statistics to pinpoint classes of genomic elements that are either enriched for or depleted regarding loci influencing a specific trait, with the model inherently accommodating multiple annotation types. Applying this approach to GWAS data for 16 human traits—including red cell indices, metabolic levels, psychiatric conditions, and stature—across seven populations reveals several annotation categories linked to these traits. By integrating known biological priors, the results for several traits, particularly psychiatric ones, align closely with established biology. Furthermore, our method identifies genomic loci enriched for affected association signals and the functional genomic profiles inherent to these locations, a case study on the *HBB* locus demonstrates is decoupled from its depletion of enhancer annotations, ultimately confirming the value of the depleted annotations in explaining the phenotype. Beyond confirming prior hypotheses, this framework offers a pragmatic, cost-effective, and high-resolution alternative to large-scale functional genomics efforts for identifying disease-causing variants. However, we also highlight potential biases in current annotation systems that could influence GWAS interpretations, suggesting prioritized lists of candidate variants for rigorous experimental validation in model organisms. We conclude by proposing extensions of this framework to annotate populations with specific phenotypes and to locate causal variants for complex traits.

Although the genetic determinants of human complexity are being uncovered, the phenotypes associated with the majority of loci identified for both monogenic and complex traits remain uncharacterized. A primary obstacle to linking genotype to phenotype is determining which genomic positions are subject to precise regulatory control. This study utilizes a novel, cost-effective approach to assess the functional importance of variants causing loss of heterozygosity in trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) patients, relying on existing annotations of gene expression in models and human tissues, protein interaction networks, and the predicted impact of variants on gene structure. We validate the phenotypes associated with these causal positions in Down syndrome and also account for a significant fraction of non-coding variants shown to cause loss of heterozygosity in the condition. Our analysis indicates that enhancer annotations, enriched for repressed associations in trisomy 21, drive the molecular pathophysiology of the disorder. We pinpoint ~200 high-priority candidate causal non-coding variants, including those near *KLF14*, which have been experimentally verified to cause overexpression of distal genes in Down syndrome models. Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that if the typical recurrence time for these systems were only around three years, as frequently asserted in the literature without explicit quantitative support, MAXI would have detected at least one source among the Galactic Centre's neutron star LMXBs every year over the past ten years—contradicting actual observations. We attribute the variability of these systems to changes in their companion star accretion rates driven by Galactic tides, which account for the full spectrum of reported recurrence times from a year to several centuries across various studies. We argue that adopting a model of recurrent but non-outbursting neutron stars to estimate the Galactic black hole population is unjustified, given the lack of evidence for the specific recurrence times required. Instead, we propose that the true population of Galactic neutron star LMXBs is likely several times larger than currently known and may include a fraction of systems that never activate on human timescales.

vibrational modes within molecules and crystals. We demonstrate that the circular motion of ions generates inertial influences on electrons. Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Enhancing these effects could establish a promising platform for manipulating localized quantum states or chemical reaction barriers through vibrational control. This framework, termed 'vibrational mechanics,' offers a fresh perspective on bridging quantum and chemical phenomena.

We have numerically modeled these rotating objects to determine whether they can sustain nuclear fusion as their energy source, accounting for significant rotational deformation rather than assuming slow rotation. For various angular momentum values, we derived critical curves in the mass versus central degeneracy parameter space where nuclear energy generation equals surface luminosity. Our results indicate that when angular momentum surpasses a threshold of $J_0=8.85\times 10^{48}$~erg~s, the critical curves split into two branches representing lower and higher degeneracy parameters at a given mass, signifying the onset of mass-shedding rotation. These findings hold practical significance for determining the maximum spin rates of fast-rotating white dwarfs and rapidly spinning brown dwarfs. Furthermore, our results align well with existing literature on slow-rotating objects and enable the exploration of brown dwarf properties amidst increasing observational data from fast-rotating populations. Ultimately, this study provides a foundational understanding of the structure and stability of rapidly rotating brown dwarfs and white dwarfs, facilitating the interpretation of current data and the analysis of new observations from missions such as TESS and CHEOPS.

This paper surveys traditional approaches for estimating efficiency and background distributions while introducing density estimation techniques based on Gaussian processes and artificial neural networks. Although these methods are widely applied in other fields, they remain underutilized in amplitude analyses. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings does not always enhance the graph's overall readability. This study examines bipartite graphs with exactly three crossings and identifies all such graphs that lack a canonical canonical crossing sequence (CCS). When canonical crossing sequences are assigned to the remaining bipartite graphs with three crossings, a canonical contact drawing emerges, which minimizes both contacts and the total number of crossings. This approach yields canonical drawings for bipartite graphs featuring three crossings from specific families. Furthermore, this work establishes several properties regarding the reduction of triple crossings into three contacts and two crossings, and it derives properties for the canonical contact drawing of bipartite graphs with three crossings by analyzing reductions that transform three contacts into either a sharp angle contact, a short edge contact, or an endpoint contact. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to a population mostly choosing one task depends intricately on the remaining prior probability mass and the relationship between the means of the two distributions; in such cases, the best response may strictly prefer the more difficult task over the easier one. These discoveries offer an intuitively optimal regulatory mechanism for agent population size aimed at minimizing completion costs and provide a robust approximation algorithm requiring only the expectation of the larger drawn difficulty, which can be effectively learned from data. To our knowledge, this work addresses the first coordination challenge where the drawn difficulty is non-uniform and not independently observable. Along the way, we contribute a theoretical framework for analyzing equilibria in continuous games and develop an ɛ-Nash approximation algorithm for cost minimization problems where agents possess incomplete information about random task difficulties. Our results are validated through both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments.

Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into horizontal and vertical frameworks; however, these standard setups often fall short in practical applications. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel fully decentralized (DF) federated learning system tailored for image classification. In this DF environment, every participant acts both as a client and a server, engaging in double-sided model collaboration to enhance the final predictive performance. Because image datasets vary significantly in dimensionality and complexity compared to tabular data, this DF setup is essential for many real-world scenarios. Although double-sided collaboration theoretically accelerates model training, it concurrently expands the attack surface, particularly within resilient but naive deep neural networks (DNNs). These DNNs are frequently exploited via data-independent adversarial examples (AEs), which are adversarially perturbed inputs designed to mislead the label prediction of a target participant. This study investigates three distinct attack paradigms within the proposed DF federated learning framework. First, we detail the setup before introducing our three attack models: Single Participant Attack (SPA), Cycle Participant Attack (CPA), and Multi Participant Attack (MPA). Additionally, we evaluate the impact of privacy-protective techniques, specifically Gaussian noise and differential privacy (DP), on both attack success and intensity. Our experimental results comprehensively assess the efficacy of these attacks under various noise conditions and provide comparative analysis against standard FL setups. Finally, we outline several promising future research directions concerning DF federated learning and adversarial robustness. To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. Furthermore, the technique is not limited to the Fourier distribution; it can be applied to any basis function combined with a probability distribution to derive efficient kernel approximations. Having established this robust three-qubit protocol, the paper outlines how it can be scaled to any chain length, either by concatenating this pulse or by interleaving it with standard $X_{1/2}$ pulses, with recommendations to prioritize standard pulses in very long chains to minimize spatially dependent frequency errors. The core methodology is straightforward: given a baseline $N$-gram model $M_B$, a neural model $M_N$ is trained to forecast the gap between the true data distribution $P$ and $M_B$. During inference, the final probability distribution is computed as $P(X) \approx M_B(X) + M_N(X \mid x_{-i}, y)$. We evaluate this method on three tasks and observe consistent gains over strong baseline models. Key contributions include a significant improvement in machine translation (a 0.75 BLEU increase over the baseline on WMT14 news), enhanced summarization performance, and a demonstration that domain adaptation can be achieved without training by utilizing a domain-specific $N$-gram model. Our code is open-source.

Recent advances in natural language processing have been driven by the success of neural language modeling, which has seen comparisons to traditional $N$-gram models in recent years. Our work builds on these observations. We conducted experiments on language modeling, machine translation, and abstraction tasks, consistently achieving performance gains with our proposed framework. The method is highly practical, allowing for domain adaptation through the use of a domain-specific $N$-gram model with no extra training required. We encourage further research into this direction and provide our code via the link below.

This model incorporates conformally coupled scalar fields alongside fundamental matter fields localized either on the boundary branes or within the bulk of the extra dimension. Our analysis focuses on generating appropriate light Higgs and dark matter masses while ensuring compatibility with observed cosmological data, specifically those related to primordial perturbations. Working within the Sakharov approach allows us to derive both the UV and renormalized IR Lagrangians, facilitating the calculation of effective field parameters. These parameters are directly linked to observable quantities such as the spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio. Our findings indicate that an $\alpha$-attractor class of models can emerge in the UV regime and realize de Sitter inflation followed by dark energy in the IR, a sequence made possible through conformal symmetry. Specifically, we identify pairs of $\alpha$-attractor potentials capable of producing the correct light masses for the Higgs and dark matter sectors. Among these, the standard single-field Starobinsky model appears as a specific instance. We assess the feasibility of detecting these model parameters through future experiments and discuss the underlying theoretical mechanisms driving these phenomenological outcomes. Our results suggest that incorporating conformal symmetry and Sakharov-induced gravity provides a robust framework for linking early and late-time cosmological events.

This study formulates and solves a century-long optimization model to determine the optimal storage deployment over time. By adjusting key parameters—including surface pressure, Coriolis force strength, solar irradiance, and surface friction—the model generates a series of steady, symmetric circulation regimes. These results are displayed in an irradiance-Coriolis parameter space as zig-zag lines known as circulation boundaries, which delineate transitions between distinct circulation patterns. The UT-ESM serves as a practical tool for exploring theoretical concepts regarding global circulation boundary formation. Crucially, this research clarifies that secondary circulation boundaries, such as the double Hadley and Ferrel cells, emerge locally rather than globally, and it provides insights into the structural differences between these friction-associated boundaries and those rooted in baroclinic instability. Finally, the paper offers qualitative explanations for each circulation boundary and quantitative analyses of the flow and thermal structures characterizing the resulting circulation regimes. Through this approach, simple yet significant findings are established regarding global atmospheric circulation boundary formation, providing a foundation for future investigations into similar phenomena with more complex models. The friction-associated secondary circulation boundaries described here are not exclusive to the UT-ESM; similar boundaries are likely present in current state-of-the-art General Circulation Models (GCMs) simulating real-world conditions, although they remain elusive due to competing physical processes and higher levels of atmospheric chaos. Consequently, this finding suggests novel methodologies for evaluating the realism of contemporary atmospheric GCMs.

AL is particularly valuable in large-scale industrial settings where labeling expenses are high, prompting practitioners to utilize every capability available to reduce the number of labeled samples. Recently, DNNs augmented with attention mechanisms have gained significant attention for their ability to highlight informative features within input data to facilitate learning. This paper introduces a novel approach that integrates a sample-level attention mechanism into AL, leveraging the learned attention weights as a non-concave importance weighting function within a variational inference (VI) framework. By employing a mixture of Gaussians (MoG) as the variational distribution, our model can closely approximate the true posterior distribution. Through case studies on synthetic and real-world industrial datasets, we demonstrate that our model outperforms current state-of-the-art AL techniques using comparable attention mechanisms. A central challenge in this endeavor is ensuring that donors occupy consistent lattice positions throughout the crystal. We address this by proposing a novel, high-throughput method to locate and map occupied donor sites across entire high-purity phosphorus-doped silicon wafers. First, we demonstrate how to attain the maximum donor concentration (approximately 10^15 cm^-3) without significantly compromising lattice uniformity or future site selection flexibility. This is achieved by carefully regulating thermal donor impurities and carefully navigating the competing competing lattice sites between the zincblende and diamond structures. Consequently, the known high-fidelity positions remain evenly distributed throughout the wafer. To illustrate the method's sensitivity and precision in identifying and characterizing these positions, we present a case study focusing on the ^{31}P isotope. Finally, we show how to determine the precise coordinates (x, y, z) of any occupied lattice site with nanometer-level accuracy using non-destructive techniques. This approach relies on analyzing the symmetry breaking of exciton transitions induced by surface steps (z) and diamond/zincblende domain boundaries (x, y). Notably, this process requires no destructive cross-sectional imaging or nano-fabrication. Our findings offer a fresh perspective on wafer-scale quantum donor experiments and significantly accelerate the path from single-qubit high fidelity to multi-qubit network functionality. This work utilizes the previously introduced high-symmetry photoluminescence spectra as the diagnostic tool. Our results advance existing knowledge regarding wafer-scale donor site density, z-position resolution, and the non-destructive nature of the process. Ultimately, this methodology provides a robust framework for accelerating quantum computing development in the donor-based silicon platform.

This study provides the initial evidence for a quantized resistance of $h/2e^2$ at $\nu=0$ in micron-scale samples and demonstrates that this value corresponds to the quantum of resistance for a quantum system possessing time-reversal symmetry.

To assess trustworthiness, we must first define it conceptually. We define trustworthiness as the degree to which an individual attributes a machine with human-like qualities—specifically intention, emotion, and reason—based on the machine's behavioral output. This stands in contrast to accuracy, which merely evaluates correct performance without considering the individual's reaction to that performance. We further distinguish our framework by demonstrating that machine-like outcomes (such as error messages) yield lower trust levels than human-like outcomes (such as emotional text), even when both are correct. Consequently, we present formulas for calculating both trust and trust enhancement, offering a clear framework to measure improvements via the difference between enhanced and original trust values. Consequently, to boost model trustworthiness, it suffices to optimize these outcomes; this can be achieved using any existing methods designed to maximize trustworthiness, including reinforcement learning, hyperparameter tuning, transfer learning, or ensemble approaches. We illustrate these concepts with examples and case studies to provide a straightforward framework for evaluating and enhancing machine trustworthiness, thereby creating a clearer pathway to trustworthy AI.

The analysis focuses on events containing precisely one isolated electron or muon alongside a minimum of four jets, based on a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 174 nb$^{-1}$. The observed $t\bar{t}$ signal exceeds the background-only hypothesis by more than five standard deviations. The resulting cross section of $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 45 \pm 8$ nb contradicts predictions derived from proton-proton collision data. Furthermore, the fractional contribution of gluons within the nucleus to protons-nuclei interactions is estimated at approximately 1% of the valence quark contribution. This cross section estimate is roughly four times larger than predictions made by various theoretical models. Additionally, the rapidity distribution of top quarks displays a slight enhancement towards negative values. These findings indicate that both the production rate and the kinematic characteristics of top quarks vary depending on the opposing particle in the collision. Consequently, the assumption that proton-proton cross sections and rapidity distributions remain unchanged when extended to proton-nucleus or nucleus-nucleus collisions is invalid. These observations carry significant implications for theoretical models describing hadron-hadron interactions and for the interpretation of cosmic-ray data. Notably, this process could be detectable in current high-luminosity proton-nucleus experiments at the Fermilab Fixed Target Facility, the CERN SPS, or at cosmic-ray interactions at the Auger and Telescope Array experiments. This detectability highlights the necessity of incorporating top-quark production into air shower simulations used for Auger and TAirGroup analyses. However, current top-quark production models fail to accurately describe the observed rapidity distribution in proton-nucleus collisions, suggesting that improvements are required to correctly interpret future air shower measurements. Potential indications of a rapidity asymmetry warrant further investigation through dedicated analyses of high-luminosity proton-nucleus data. It is also possible that certain beyond-the-Standard-Model asymmetries, unobservable in proton-proton collisions, could be detected via air shower experiments. These results rely on the latest proton-nucleus nuclear modification factors and enhance our understanding of the internal structure of nuclei.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown significant promise in generating explanations for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Building on this trend, we investigate the potential of LLMs to explain semantic parsing into SQL. Our results indicate that mainstream models struggle to accurately explain TPT (Table-Driven Parser)-executable SQL for complex queries, frequently producing errors such as missing columns, incorrect table joins, and misplaced filter conditions. Although few-shot prompting helps address missing column issues, it often leads to an explosion in hallucinated values. To mitigate these challenges, we propose a post-processing method that utilizes an internal LLM evaluator to correct hallucinated values. We collected a new dataset of approximately 3,000 examples from BigQuery to train a BERT-based model for evaluating the correctness of selected table columns. Our findings reveal that accurate table selection is critical for LLMs to reduce hallucinations and improve overall execution accuracy. We also discovered that combining few-shot prompts with in-context examples drawn from the same dataset yields superior results. This approach yields an average execution accuracy of 76.5% on a complex query subset and 70.5% on all queries, surpassing a zero-shot baseline by 11.0% in execution accuracy and 16.0% in exact set match accuracy. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/MuShang0327/LLM-SQL-Explanation.

Formulating DP for graphs is challenging because data points are interconnected, often in non-isomorphic ways, which complicates the definition of neighbor relationships necessary for standard DP mechanisms like noisy aggregation. To address these challenges, we categorize DP graph problems into three types based on the level of noise added to the output: private input (standard DP), private output (functional/utility DP), and private intermediate steps (process/functional differential privacy). This framework encompasses a wide range of graph analysis tasks, from publishing graph metrics to training GNNs. We evaluate current state-of-the-art methods across these problem categories and outline several open research questions in the field. By providing a comprehensive overview of private graphs, we aim to facilitate future work on the privacy-preserving analysis graph-structured data. Graphs are ubiquitous, serving as foundational data structures across numerous domains and enabling the analysis of complex systems and phenomena. However, applying differential privacy (DP) to graph-related problems remains an active area of research with significant potential impact. This survey offers a comprehensive guide to private graphs, categorizing problems into three types based on where privacy is enforced: private input (private graph nodes/edges), private output (graph statistics), and private intermediate steps (graph learning models). We review state-of-the-art approaches for private graphs, provide a guided overview of private graph node and attribute privacy, and discuss open challenges in private graph analysis. By summarizing recent advancements and highlighting key open problems, this survey provides a solid foundation for further research into the privacy of graph-based data. This review examines the potential scientific outcomes and prospects of Euclid across diverse domains, including the evolution of galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGN), the local and early Universe, Milky Way and stellar population studies, supernovae and transients, Solar System objects, exoplanets, strong gravitational lensing, and galaxy clusters. In this study, we develop a novel hydrodynamic model capable of capturing the non-Gaussian characteristics inherent in certain quantum systems. Building on this advanced framework, we successfully investigate both the unitary evolution following sudden quenchs and evolution driven by external fields in a quantum Heisenks chain. A key contribution of our work is demonstrating how the proposed hydrodynamic equations enable the accurate tracking of crucial quantum metrics—specifically typicality and scrambling—through their quantum current distributions.
