While the depth-averaged Navier--Stokes (DA NS) equations offer higher precision than the Saint-Venant (SV) equations by accounting fluid viscosity, their computational cost is prohibitive for the high-resolution mesh networks needed in flood forecasting. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel numerical method that leverages DA NS viscosity terms as regularizers, enabling the solution of the inviscid DA NS equations with kinetics energy regularization at the resolution of the shallow water equations. Since the 1990s, the regularization/nesting technique has been widely adopted to resolve turbulent flows using the kinetic energy (KE) of two-dimensional large-eddy simulation (LES) equations as a regularizer for the cost-effective Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) turbulence model. Building on this history, this paper extends the method to three-dimensional (3D) turbulence by regularizing the RANS model with the turbulent KE of 3D LES. Although this increases computational cost due to the complexity of 3D filtering, we significantly reduce it by employing a coarse filtering grid derived from the existing RANS model grid. Validation against 3D direct numerical simulation (DNS) data from a flat-plate boundary layer shows that the results match 3D DNS kinetics energy very closely, with turbulent energy, Reynolds shear stress, and mean velocity aligning well with DNS results away from the wall. Compared to traditional 2D nesting, the 3D version offers similar advantages in computational cost and accuracy. However, discrepancies with 3D DNS near the wall suggest areas for future improvement, such as utilizing higher-resolution filtering grids, developing smaller eddy viscosity models (EVM), or increasing subgrid-scale (SGS) viscosity near the wall. This category represents the most fundamental class of maps adhering to a version of the $h$-principle; in two dimensions, it closely approximates oriented submersions, as every such map of dimension 2 targeting a closed, simply connected manifold is bordant to a submersion. We demonstrate that the Madsen-Weiss theorem (the standard Mumford Conjecture) operates within a broader framework of the $h$-principle. Specifically, a version of the $h$-principle for oriented colored broken submersions, when combined with the Harer stability theorem and the Miller-Morita theorem, yields the Madsen-Weiss theorem. Furthermore, the Miller-Morita theorem is shown to be equivalent to the $h$-principle for these maps. This provides a new and more accessible proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, utilizing a result by Karamov and Vartanov which asserts that any morse function targetable by an oriented colored broken submersion is $V$-trivial. Additionally, we offer a new characterization of the 3-dimensional Poincaré Conjecture in terms of the $h$-principle for oriented colored broken submersions. The paper also includes a section dedicated to explaining the components of this principle and a final section detailing related findings by the author.

This study examines the dispersion of particles or pathogens traveling via jumping animals across a fractured ground composed of tiles with varying sizes. The motion is modeled such that individuals move from one location to another only if they are on the same animal, allowing for non-Gaussian behavior and potentially super-diffusive scaling. We analyze this system using both continuous media approximations and discrete models, deriving analytical expressions for the mean square displacement that align with numerical simulations across all temporal and spatial scales. Our findings indicate a bifurcation in the asymptotic regime based on a specific exponent governing the tile size distribution. For values below a critical threshold, the system exhibits a front-like profile with exponential decay and a super-diffusive trajectory described by a non-Gaussian curve; otherwise, an exponential decay profile and diffusive behavior are observed. These results offer insights into the spatial distribution of active zones within disordered media and provide potential explanations for front propagation in infected areas, provided agents adhere to residual connectivity along these fronts. Ultimately, we establish that such phenomena arise from the interplay between the agents' mobility statistics and the obstacle disorder. The approach is generalized to scenarios involving two competing species with distinct jumping ranges, addressing issues of competition, exclusion, and coexistence. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that competition drives a transition from diffusion to ballistic motion, ultimately leading to the exclusion of the less mobile species. Throughout the paper, competing random walkers are employed to model various exclusion processes, including the KMP model (equivalent to Dvoretzky's exchange process), the asymmetric simple exclusion process, and the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process. Along the way, we derive analytical formulas for mean square displacements that validate numerical findings and simplify the understanding of dynamical mechanisms leading to ballistic regimes. This regime is characterized by the "fingers" formed by the range of the walkers imposed upon the randomness of the ground fracture. Finally, we discuss potential extensions, including particle diffusion through porous media and competitive scenarios involving predatory animals. These simple yet significant models yield strikingly non-intuitive outcomes regarding the regimes governing the motion of jumping animals and the dynamics of competing species.

Multi-task self-supervised pretraining is essential for overcoming the barriers associated with single-task learning and supervised approaches in complex, real-world contexts. However, existing research often focuses on narrow actions rather than meaningful objectives, and the automatic generation of diverse tasks remains a significant hurdle. To address this, we employed hierarchical world modeling combined with inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn objectives and their corresponding actions. This strategy enabled us to autonomously identify and execute diverse tasks for life skills, removing the need for human supervision during the training phase. Furthermore, life skills are semantically related; therefore, we applied a cross-task attention mechanism within a multi-task pretraining framework to leverage data efficiency by sharing information among similar tasks. Experimental results across various domains show that MS2Life successfully learns multiple life skills, including stacking, pouring, and playing with Legos, and demonstrates superior generalization, fine-tuning efficiency, and performance compared to baseline methods. (Video available at https://ms2life.github.io/)

Recovery from model bias and underfitting in decision-making systems is difficult, particularly when training data is limited. We investigate the feasibility of training policies using only local world models and a global policy optimizer without direct environmental interaction. Our findings indicate that world models can serve as an effective data augmentation technique, and strategically combining them with the actual environment during self-supervised pretraining enhances data efficiency. Additionally, we designed a life skill taxonomy to address the challenge of automatic task generation. (Video available at https://ms2life.github.io/)

Abstract -- This paper presents an automated system for creating and evaluating English grammar exercises using artificial intelligence. The system features a user-friendly interface that requires no programming knowledge, making it accessible for exercise developers, students, and teachers. Its primary application lies in language education, where it generates exercises and assessments based on input grammar rules and sentence fragments. Comparative analysis was conducted between human-created baseline exercises and those generated by the proposed system. We note that training is hindered by a skewed relationship proposal distribution, where most negative proposals are easily detected due to inaccurate object detection, causing the model to underfit rare, difficult cases. To address this, we introduce Spatially-Aware Balanced negative pRoposal sAmpling (SABRA), a robust VRD framework designed to mitigate false positive impacts. Authors address complaints regarding false positive predictions in the VRD task by comparing positive and negative samples drawn randomly from the remaining data after filtering known object pairs. They construct a complex loss function and loss function of record to optimize the model against this "adversarial" negative distribution. However, the model may simply learn to fit this specific distribution without genuinely improving performance, and the proposed weak supervision method risks over-smoothing global negative information. The proposed methods also fail to directly target the true core issue: the imbalanced distribution of rare relationships. Consequently, there is a risk that the approach may not effectively enhance the model's ability to detect challenging relationships. The evaluation on the VRD dataset is considered insufficient, as the testset lacks ground truth labels and likely contains biases toward popular relationships, making it a suboptimal benchmark for assessing false positive rates. Additionally, the evaluation on the VRET dataset is inconclusive because many true positive relationships still receive low confidence scores, indicating that the model's performance improvement is not fully satisfactory. Overall, the contribution feels marginal, the methodology is complex, and the empirical validation is not robust enough to support the core claim regarding the primary cause of false positives. These galaxies exhibit two distinct characteristics: (1) their infrared luminosity significantly exceeds that predicted by the main sequence relation, and (2) they display unusually flat, nearly featureless continuum spectra. While these traits are frequently observed in $z>2$ clusters, this represents the highest cluster environment in which they have been identified. The flat continuum suggests that intense starbursts are obscured by strong dust attenuation and may indicate that these galaxies possess compact structures. Utilizing galaxy evolution models, we determine that these systems have formed the majority of their stellar mass through major mergers with other star-forming galaxies within the cluster. Furthermore, these objects are poorly represented by standard galaxy formation simulations, implying that current models lack critical physical components necessary to accurately reproduce massive cluster galaxies throughout cosmic history. Given their rarer nature compared to typical starbursts at similar redshifts, these galaxies may offer insights into the future evolution of massive galaxies within the local cluster environment. However, further observational and theoretical work is necessary to fully understand the formation history and physical properties of these objects. Notably, the source with the greatest infrared excess also exhibits the weakest [OIII] emission line detection among the trio, suggesting that the dominant feedback mechanism driving evolution in the most infrared-luminous galaxies may differ from that in the others. These findings were published by D. A. Swinbank et al. (MNRAS, 2013).

While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, displays a surface rotation rate exceeding that of its bulk envelope, contradicting standard angular momentum conservation expectations. We enhance the spectroscopic constraints on the surface rotation, confirm that pulsation frequencies align with previously determined core and envelope rotation rates, and establish that the star lacks significant chemical peculiarities. Furthermore, we evaluate evidence against the presence of a tidally interacting companion. Finally, we explore possible origins for this anomalous rotation profile, such as the accretion of a giant planet or anomalous angular momentum transport via tidal inertial waves driven by a close substellar companion, and advocate for additional observational and theoretical investigations. KIC 9267654 offers a pliable platform for theoretical modeling and potential contrasts with numerically simulated rotation profiles. As a bright, relatively slow-rotating giant star with precisely known internal constraints, it is well-suited for studying the gyrochronology break, the tidal inertial-wave spectrum, the accretion of planets onto rotating stars, or the generation of differential rotation through convection and magnetic braking.

Omni-directional precoding is a promising technique for expanding wireless network coverage. This approach requires orthogonal training sequences, making the selection of complementary codes critical. Currently, Golay complementary pairs and quads are recognized as optimal complementary code sets with zero side-lobes. However, these codes are limited by specific size constraints. To address this limitation, this work utilizes Golay complementary matrix (GCM) quads, which offer greater design freedom. We propose using GCM quads with array dimensions $s_1\times s_2\times s_3$ to determine the deployment sizes of three base stations in an omni-directional precoding system. We also examine size constraints for quaternary GCM quads and present several numerical examples. To our knowledge, this application of GCM quads represents a novel concept. Our analysis reveals that GCM quads are feasible for quaternary complementary factors summing to 24, with individual sizes not exceeding 16. Omni-directional precoding systems can thus be implemented using complementary factors that sum to 24, except for the specific dimension constraint of 16x16x16. These results advance the development of complementary codes for omni-directional precoding.

Although graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a valuable relational inductive bias for modeling these systems, research into their ability to generalize to new instances within the same system type remains limited. In this study, we trained GNNs to learn time series data from a specific nonlinear dynamical system known as the belief propagation algorithm. Complex systems are characterized by numerous components and their relationships, making graph-based representations a popular approach to represent them. However, developing new network data often relies on expensive or unreliable human expertise. Inspired by the structure of probabilistic inference, we introduce a framework for inferring system structure through its dynamics using time series observations. This approach draws inspiration from existing methods for learning complex system structure from time series, particularly Gaussian systems like belief propagation (BP). We demonstrate that our method can reconstruct the full structure of a target system, including long-range interactions absent in simple lattice models, solely from time series data of node states. Furthermore, once the structure is inferred, it can be used to initialize a BP model that generalizes accurately when applied to previously unseen nodes of the system. These results indicate that the underlying dynamics of complex systems encode information necessary for inferring their structure. This work promotes understanding complex systems via their dynamics and encourages the design of new systems by leveraging the generalization properties of probabilistic inference models. Our framework is domain-agnostic regarding both the systems being built and those under investigation, allowing it to be applied to a wide range of complex systems. Code is available at https://github.com/andrewg519/belief-inference.

Recent years have witnessed a dramatic advancement in video technology, yielding extensive video repositories. Concurrently, video description has gained significant traction due to its broad range of applications, such as enabling visually impaired users to comprehend video content and offering marketing insights through popular item summaries. Although existing approaches have yielded encouraging results, they often struggle with specific video segments, as action-based descriptions are inherently more concise and precise than scene-based ones. Consequently, this paper introduces a novel task: action-oriented video description (AOVD). We propose a cross-modal framework that synergistically leverages external action description data, LSTMs for sequence modeling, and attention mechanisms to produce accurate action-based summaries. Experimental results across several public benchmarks confirm the model's efficacy and surpass current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, ablation studies provide empirical validation for the proposed approach. As this is the inaugural work to define AOVD, subsequent research can further explore this actionable video description domain. The source code is available at https://github.com/yzh1997/AOVD.

To address this limitation, we introduce a BERT-based cross-lingual text classification model (Bi-CAM) that integrates pseudolingual knowledge transfer with bidirectional cross-lingual attention mechanisms. Although Group Lasso is a recognized efficient method for selecting both continuous and categorical variables, it often yields distinct estimates for each level of a selected factor, resulting in non-sparse fitted models that are hard to interpret. To achieve sparsity with Group Lasso, we propose a two-step approach: first, use Group Lasso to reduce data dimensionality; second, select the final model by applying an information criterion to a restricted set of models generated by clustering the levels of individual factors. We evaluate the algorithm's selection accuracy in sparse, high-dimensional settings and test it on both synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of prediction accuracy and model dimensionality. Furthermore, our method identifies interactions driven by specific levels of factors that other algorithms fail to detect, a capability highlighted through a detailed analysis of factors influencing liver transplant eligibility. This two-step method is implemented in the R package `sparsGroupLasso`, available at: https://github.com/MohsenGhoreishi/sparsGroupLasso.

This study introduces a technique to embed structured knowledge into LLMs by directly training T5 models on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs. Our results demonstrate that T5 models pre-trained on Wikidata using this approach surpass standard baselines on FreebaseQA, WikiHop, and specific subsets of TriviaQA and NaturalQuestions. Furthermore, models trained on factual triples perform comparably to those trained on natural language sentences containing identical information. When applied to the smaller WikiMovies dataset, our method achieved a threefold increase in exact match scores on the MetaQA task relative to the T5 baseline. A key benefit of this approach is that it eliminates the need for aligning knowledge graphs with text corpora during data preparation, rendering it especially advantageous for industry-scale knowledge graphs. To facilitate this, we provide access to a WikiMovies knowledge graph formatted for training and a WikiMovie question answering model that exceeds the performance of the T5 baseline. We also observe that model performance correlates strongly with the density of the knowledge graph. Our method offers a straightforward strategy for incorporating structured knowledge during pre-training that can be readily adapted to various structured data types. However, additional research is needed to evaluate this approach on larger datasets and different model architectures, as well as on internal knowledge retention using evaluation frameworks beyond question answering. This technique can be easily implemented by integrating known triples into a data loading pipeline and training on a formatted knowledge graph in triplets.

LLMs trained on web crawl data struggle to retain knowledge because valuable information is dispersed across numerous documents, making it difficult for evaluators to assess their internalized knowledge. We introduce a framework to measure the internalized knowledge of LLMs using a new evaluation set called ReTeLL (Retrieval-less Text Evaluation for LLMs), composed of factually accurate summaries derived from automatically scraped Wikipedia pages. ReTeLL offers two key advantages: it allows for the assessment of internalized knowledge without the confounding factor of learned retrieval capabilities, and it can be constructed for any domain. Our findings indicate that current LLMs struggle to learn knowledge from Wikipedia, performing worse on ReTeLL than on WikiQA, a benchmark they have already trained on. Additionally, we show that T5 models trained explicitly on factual triples from knowledge graphs achieve significant gains over the baseline on ReTeLL and that Wikilinks serve as a rich semantic resource for model training. Because the OpenGL API has limitations, a standard approach involves splicing multiple triangles at different scales to approximate fan-shaped joins, a method that often results in unrealistic artifacts and suboptimal rendering speeds. To address these issues, this paper introduces a simple yet efficient algorithm that replaces the multi-triangle approximation with just two triangles. By dividing long sequences into smaller segments and utilizing both intra-chunk and inter-chunk RNNs, the DPRNN achieved significant performance improvements while maintaining a compact model size. Building on this, we integrate the DPRNN module with a Convolution Recurrent Network (CRN) to create the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), specifically designed for time-frequency domain speech enhancement. This approach is appealing because it relies on fundamental dynamics, thereby circumventing the invalid assumptions found in mass-flux convection schemes at current resolutions. Nevertheless, the optimal closure strategies for multi-fluid equations governing atmospheric convection remain unclear. This study develops a straightforward single-column model featuring two fluids—one rising and one falling—without incorporating additional sub-filter variability modeling. When applied to Rayleigh-Bénard convection, the model demonstrates that minimal closures suffice to predict the correct scaling of heat flux (Nu) across six orders of magnitude in buoyancy forcing (Ra). These findings indicate that even a rudimentary two-fluid model can effectively capture the primary coherent overturning structures of convection. Consequently, resolving these features in larger-scale models would likely yield improvements over current multi-fluid closures, potentially making such systems viable for resolving overturning clouds at satellite imagery resolutions. The proposed closure's computational efficiency and robustness suggest its utility in exploring the statistical properties of turbulent convection using large-eddy simulations. Ultimately, this study affirms the feasibility of resolving 3D overturning clouds in global models, thereby advancing efforts to accurately model convective clouds in future climate research.

We analyze the conditions required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. Our results indicate that this process is unattainable if the cavities interacting with the uncorrelated atoms share classical correlations with any other cavity. However, we observe that the atomic states can become genuinely multipartite entangled if the cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with another cavity. This non-trivial finding offers a potential method for generating multipartite entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions and can be implemented using existing experimental setups. This approach offers significant advantages over traditional methods that rely on direct cavity-cavity coupling or photon exchange between cavities connected by optical fibers. This work contributes to the field of quantum information processing by providing a practical protocol for creating multipartite entangled atoms within current experimental frameworks. This research builds upon previous studies regarding Jaynes-Cummings dynamics and multipartite quantum correlations, referencing works by Mathew et al. (Quantum Inf. Process. 15, 3605, 2016) and Mathew (Quantum Inf. Process. 18, 63, 2019).

Active learning (AL) significantly enhances the efficiency of text classification by strategically selecting the most informative samples for human annotation within a limited budget. This work compares two state-of-the-art AL methods—Rule-based Active Learning (RL) and a Rule-based Active Learning framework (RALF)—against a broad spectrum of existing active learning techniques across three benchmark datasets. Our findings indicate that both RL and RALF consistently outperform traditional AL approaches, with RL showing particularly strong performance on the smaller dataset. Furthermore, we analyze how rule system quality impacts the effectiveness of rule-based methods and compare our results with semi-supervised learning strategies. Source code is provided at https://github.com/ahmed-alsalem/RuleBasedAL. This paper earned the Best Paper Award at ICACSI-CONvIT 2019.

Automatic summarization aims to extract the core message from source text, a task that has recently attracted significant research interest. While numerous models have been proposed for news article summarization, there is a lack of focused work on tweet-based news summarization. This paper introduces a sequence-to-sequence model enhanced with attention mechanisms and encoder/decoder convolutional neural networks (LSTM and Bi-LSTM) specifically for tweet news summarization. Comparative evaluation against state-of-the-art models using an existing evaluation metric confirms the superior performance of our proposed solution. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-alsalem/SummModel. This work received the Best Paper Award at ICACSI-CONvIT 2019.

This study examines the connection between the observable shadow radius and the first-order phase transition of non-linear charged AdS black holes within the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. The analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, the shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature (or pressure) exhibit non-monotonic behaviors. Furthermore, from the perspective of the shadow radius, the phase transition temperature is higher than that derived from the horizon radius under identical conditions. These findings suggest that the shadow radius serves as an effective probe for uncovering thermodynamic phase transition details in black holes. Additionally, thermal profiles illustrating the coexistence of big and small black hole phases during phase transitions are presented for two distinct non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter values ($\gamma=1$ and $\gamma=1.5$). Finally, the influence of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter on both the shadow radius and thermal profiles is further explored. Regarding theoretical significance, this work expands understanding of black hole dynamics and phase transitions by integrating non-linear Yang-Mills charge into the system. While numerous reconstruction methods exist—from conventional protocols to machine learning approaches—no single universal technique currently allows for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that nonclassical phenomena, including entanglement variations during dynamical evolution and the emergence of quantum synchronization, manifest as qualitative shifts within the optical tomograms themselves. Consequently, explicit state reconstruction is unnecessary to detect these effects. However, if one must choose only two parameters for analysis, we recommend optimizing the pair with the strongest statistical correlation: the optical tomogram and final quantum synchronization, or the optical tomogram and synchronization-induced entanglement changes. This approach requires 33% fewer measurement data points than reconstructing the Wigner function and eliminates the need for mathematical inversion during data processing. Furthermore, this strategy avoids the common issue of over-smoothing the estimated optical quantum state. These findings confirm that substantial effect estimation does not mandate full state reconstruction, as significant parameter estimates can be derived directly from the optically measurable quantum state's optical tomogram. These conclusions apply not just to the Wigner function, but to any representable optical quantum state. Although the study focuses on quantum synchronization and entanglement dynamics within continuous-variable systems, the proposed strategy is broadly applicable to estimate significant parameters in other quantum scenarios. The results are especially pertinent to contemporary experiments aiming to measure quantum synchronization or dynamical entanglement, where our strategy can significantly reduce both data acquisition volume and processing time. The essential mathematical procedures are detailed in Methods A and B. This work emphasizes that there is no universal reconstruction method for an optically measurable continuous-variable quantum state; rather, researchers should select representation techniques that minimize data volume and avoid redundant mathematical inversion. These conclusions are directly applicable to estimating Synchronization Depth, Quantum Synchronization Time, entanglement dynamics, and optical Bell inequality maximums from optical tomograms without state reconstruction. Since optical tomograms are diagonal density matrix representations, the findings also generalize to the Pauli representation. The study does not claim a breakthrough in quantum synchronization, as this field has been extensively explored since its inception. Instead, the work offers a pragmatic estimate of synchronization-related parameters that drastically cuts data requirements. A prevalent strategy to reduce bandwidth usage involves streaming only the portion of the video within the user's current viewport, a technique known as viewport-based video streaming (VVS). Recent research has indicated that hardblock effectives (HE) can further enhance bandwidth efficiency by not limiting encoded details to the viewport but instead suppressing background information where human vision is less sensitive. However, current HE approaches either compromise video quality in extensive background areas or fail to accurately predict the user's gazing direction. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a predictive hardblock effective method (PHBM). This proposed technique leverages head pose estimation (HPE) to anticipate the user's gazing direction and applies hardblock effects to regions unlikely to be viewed. Experiments conducted on real-world video data demonstrate that both HPE and PHBM are readily implementable and outperform state-of-the-art solutions. Specifically, compared to conventional HE methods, PHBM maintains higher overall video quality while excluding approximately 20% of background information. Furthermore, compared to existing predictive HE methods, PHBM more accurately predicts the user's gazing direction and eliminates an additional 15% of background data. Finally, PHBM significantly improves system bandwidth efficiency when viewed as a complete solution.

However, these methods previously lacked rigorous mathematical backing because standard approximations for thermal states and time evolution typically required a bond dimension that scales with system size. To resolve this limitation, we develop PEPOs capable of approximating thermal expectation values and Heisenberg time evolution for all local observables. The necessary bond dimension remains independent of system size, relying instead solely on temperature or time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of these constructs in estimating thermal correlation functions and expectation values following quantum quenches.

Quantum phases of matter are characterized by observable discrepancies between the ground states of different phases, often arising from symmetries and quantum entanglement, which can lead to topological phases lacking such symmetries and exhibiting robustness against perturbations. While projective quantum lattice models efficiently capture essential features of quantum many-body systems—such as scaling of ground state entropy, correlation length, and entanglement entropy—previous formulations lacked rigorous justification except when the bond dimension $D$ scales with system size $N$. We establish that symmetric MPOs enable the representation of projective quantum lattice models invariant under finite on-site symmetry groups. We show that for any such group, the bond dimension scales as $O(K^2)$, where $K$ is the group size, a significant improvement over the naive $O(KN)$ scaling. This result is achieved by constructing a canonical form for projective equivalence, proving that states within the same class are finitely many steps apart under projective unitary transformations, and developing algorithms to classify symmetry-enriched topological phases. Our findings align with recent discoveries regarding the scalings of entanglement and correlation lengths relative to $K$. Additionally, we illustrate the use of these models in solving quantum many-body problems, such as determining ground state energies and performing quantum quenches. These methods are particularly valuable for assessing the feasibility of simulating quantum many-body systems on emerging quantum computers.

Although we assume site-wise symmetry, our approach does not depend on its global conservation. The symmetric MPO formalism accommodates systems with broken symmetry, as evidenced by the emergence of degeneracy in the ground state energy scaling. We also address systems with no site-wise symmetry and provide numerical examples using the Heisenberg model to demonstrate the practical efficacy of the proposed methods.

However, simultaneously achieving the lateral nanoscale dimensions necessary for device miniaturization while retaining tunable optomagnetic properties and out-of-plane anisotropy remains a significant challenge. This study addresses this by embedding nanosized Tb$_{15}$Co$_{85}$ ferrimagnetic alloys, which possess robust out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy, into a gold plasmonic nanoantenna array. This integration creates a micrometer-scale magnetophotonic crystal that displays sharp, narrow magneto-optical spectral features, which can be precisely controlled by both external magnetic and light fields. The resulting narrow Fano-type resonance is generated through the interference between the plasmonic mode of a single antenna and a far-field continuum wave; its specific characteristics are dictated by the RE-TM alloy's density, magnetic orientation, and magnitude of anisotropy. Notably, the chiral nature of the near field within the antenna selectively influences the circular polarization of the resonance. Furthermore, the magnetized RE-TM nanoantennas function as a nonreciprocal filter for circular polarization, a phenomenon confirmed via time-resolved X-ray magnetic circular dichroism spectroscopy, which also validates the alloy's out-of-plane anisotropy and its spatial distribution. This work provides a customizable narrow resonance feature that responds to both light and magnetic fields, offering a significant advancement over current magnetophotonic crystal technologies and a promising platform for on-chip memory and sensing components.

for accelerating deep neural networks, where a compact student model learns by mimicking the softmax outputs of a high-capacity teacher model. Traditionally, this process requires access to both the training data and the teacher's internal parameters, a setup often impractical in real-world scenarios due to storage constraints or privacy concerns. To address this, we introduce Decision-Based Black-Box (DB3) knowledge distillation, which trains a student model using a black-box teacher that reveals only class labels instead of softmax probabilities. Our approach first addresses cases where training data is available: we calculate a sample's robustness against other classes by measuring its distance to the teacher's decision boundaries to generate soft labels for standard KD training. We further extend this method to scenarios where even training data access is impossible by generating pseudo-samples that are maximally distinguished by the teacher's decision boundaries, using their derived soft labels as a transfer set. Experiments across various benchmark networks and datasets confirm the effectiveness of our methods, with source code available at https://github.com/zhengjia001/DB3-KD. Our results indicate that this new framework can achieve performance within 5% of white-box KD using only training data, and approximately 10% when training data is also unavailable. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework named Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which utilizes an agent's own historical successful experiences rather than relying on external experts. Specifically, we train two distinct agents by having them alternately explore the environment and leverage the peer's past experiences. Since these experiences may range from valuable to misleading, we propose estimating their potential utility based on the expected gain of the value function. This allows agents to selectively imitate one another, prioritizing useful data while filtering out noise. Experimental results across various tasks demonstrate the significant superiority of the proposed CoIL framework, confirming that agents can mutually benefit without external supervision. Furthermore, we release our environment and implementation to accelerate future research, as the application of imitation learning without external experts offers even greater potential for the field of artificial intelligence. The source code is available at: https://github.com/hhchen0208/CoIL_Environment.

Using this proposed metric, PAC code decoding requires computational effort comparable to sequential decoding of conventional convolutional codes. Simulation results indicate enhanced error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes when employing this metric. We demonstrate that setting the polarized cutoff rate as the metric value—calculated as the average of the minimum polarized cutoff rate encountered along all paths within the search space of the sequential decoder—effectively mitigates channel polarization degradation in finite-length codes. Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach for boosting Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Nevertheless, recent studies suggest that RL's benefits in NMT largely stem from reinforcing tokens that were already highly probable during pre-training. We propose that the extensive action space is a primary barrier to RL's efficacy in machine translation and validate this hypothesis through two experimental series. First, we observe that shrinking the vocabulary size enhances RL performance. Second, we demonstrate that effectively lowering the action space dimensionality without altering the vocabulary also leads to significant gains, as measured by BLEU scores. Specifically, projecting continuous representations of target tokens instead of treating them as discrete categories allows Policy Gradient (PG) algorithms to ignore the vocabulary size. Furthermore, we find that replacing the standard encoder-decoder architecture's final fully connected layer with a matching layer for the discrete token category further enhances this approach's results. To our knowledge, this is the first time these findings have been documented for RL-enhanced NMT. Our source code is available here: https://github.com/mayaelgamal/RL-after-MLE-NMT.

Machine translation has long been limited by the computational expense of training after pre-training. Recently, efficient attention mechanisms have accelerated BERT-like NMT models by significantly cutting training FLOPs with negligible accuracy loss compared to Transformer baselines. However, these models remain limited by the high memory demands of standard BERT architectures, which store repeated source segments in the encoder's hidden states. We introduce TransBERT, a model that retains efficient translation while offering linear memory and time complexity with constant hidden states relative to source length. TransBERT achieves sub-linear memory and time usage, thanks to its sub-linear memory efficient encoder and linear time/memory efficient decoder. On WMT18 NMT tasks (German->English and English->French), TransBERT needs only 25% of the training time and 50% of the training memory of a Transformer, while achieving comparable results to larger models. Our ablation study offers insights into efficiently training and fine-tuning modern machine translation systems. TransBERT sets a compact benchmark for efficient machine translation, featuring less than linear memory and time complexity, linear memory efficient encoding, and constant hidden state dimensions throughout the model. Like the efficient encoder in the Transformer-XL language modeling architecture, TransBERT's encoder achieves linear memory and time complexity while maintaining high-quality translation by leveraging long-range source dependencies via its hidden state cache. For the decoder, TransBERT adopts the NMT architecture from Transformer-XL,

This study experimentally investigates time-discrete, periodically driven dynamics in a single photon coupled to an environment. We present a comprehensive theoretical framework that elucidates the experimental findings and provides an analytical description of the system's non-equilibrium steady states. Furthermore, we show that both the periodic driving and environmental properties can be engineered to sustain an asymptotically non-vanishing bidirectional information flow between the open system and its environment.

By leveraging the theory of recurrent tensors alongside harmonic and biharmonic maps, we also derive findings on recurrent curvature and Ricci recurrence alongside biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean geometry. in base $p/q$ is defined by a function mapping finite words over the alphabet $A_p=\{0,1,...,p-1\}$ to rational values, which satisfies specific functional equations. When $p/q$ is a ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers $F_k/F_{k-1}$, this base yields the Zeckendorf numeration system; in this case, the function is invertible, defining the bijection known as the Fibonacci coding. This paper demonstrates that the base $p/q$ function is invertible precisely when $p/q$ corresponds to a generalized Pisot number. Furthermore, we characterize the inversion formula for the base $p/q$ function using a generalized Pisot coding. These results generalize the well-documented findings for Pisot and Fibonacci base $p/q$ functions to a broader class of sequences defined by linear recurrence relations. Additionally, we provide explicit formulas for the digits of any real number within the range $[0,1]$ under the base $p/q$ coding. The main findings are presented without proofs in companion videos available at https://youtu.be/0y45y354Y88 and https://youtu.be/2y0u45y354Y88. 2012 Mathematics Subject Classification: 68Q42, 11B39. To address this challenge, we developed FindIt, a system designed to identify all document values assigned to a specific key in a MongoDB replica set. FindIt leverages the document structure of MongoDB to identify semi-joint primary keys within documents, thereby locating every occurrence of a target key. Our experimental results demonstrate that findKeys(), our algorithm for detecting the full set of primary keys in a sample of documents, is at least an order of magnitude more effective than existing approximate primary key discovery methods. Moreover, findValues(), a higher-level algorithm, surpasses standard MongoDB query operations by exceeding a 100-fold improvement in performance for well-range skewed lookup keys and achieving up to an 11,000-fold gain for point query lookups. Consequently, findKeys() and findValues() significantly outperform traditional indexing methods in scenarios involving temporary or temporary-like primary keys, making findKeys() approximately three orders of magnitude more effective than current index creation methods for such use cases. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising framework for automatically adjusting machine learning systems to live data feeds, yet prior attempts have yielded mixed results and lack a comprehensive performance evaluation. This study conducts an exhaustive analysis of existing RL approaches applied to classification problems with live feeds, highlighting their limitations through extensive empirical tests. Our findings indicate that current methods struggle with nonlinear tasks and offer no clear advantage over simple heuristic baselines. To further investigate, we built a extensive synthetic dataset generator that creates life-like time-series data for classification across various conditions. This dataset reveals performance bottlenecks in current cross-corpus adaptation efforts and exposes additional issues when models are deployed with live data. Additionally, we present RL-DA, a straightforward domain adaptation protocol based on deep RL that effectively adapts pre-trained models to real-time data feeds. RL-DA requires only around 1,000 examples for adaptation, needs less memory than heuristic alternatives, and delivers significant performance gains, improving results by over 16% compared to state-of-the-art methods. (Our code is available at https://github.com/anjaliparash/RL-Domain-Adaptation)

This analysis yields the form factor spectrum, from which four distinct form factors are derived by fitting to data using the lowest three representations of the $SU(3)_W$ weak group. The quark masses are derived from the slope of the form factor trajectory in HQE space; specifically, $\sqrt{\langle m_{b}^{2}\rangle - m_{b}^{2}}$ corresponds to the RMS fluctuation of the quark mass square. The quark mass is modeled as $m_q(v\cdot p) = M_{q}(M_W^2) + c_1(M_c^2) + \mathcal{O}(1/m_b)$, where $M_q(M_W^2)$ represents the running mass at the $Z^0$ mass scale and $m_c(v\cdot p)$ is the in-flight quark mass. The results are $m_{b}(\text{kin}) = 460^{+22}_{-21}(\text{exp})^{+4}_{-6}(\text{theory})$ MeV and $m_{c}(\text{kin}) = 1596^{+29}_{-27}(\text{exp})^{+6}_{-8}(\text{theory})$ MeV, with uncertainties arising from statistical fluctuations, the choice of QCD scale, and theoretical approximations. Additionally, the slope of the form factor trajectory in OPE parameter space is calculated via lattice QCD, confirming consistency between the experimental and theoretical determinations of quark masses. Constructed as Wronskians of standard Hermite polynomials, these polynomials are significant in mathematical physics, random matrix theory, and one-dimensional supersymmetric (SUSY) quantum mechanics. Characterized by quadratic behavior at infinity and possessing only real roots, these potentials arise from recursive relations governed by discrete parameters. We establish their solvability through the lens of shape invariance in 1D SUSY quantum mechanics. Building on this foundation, we derive their associated energy spectra and eigenfunctions. Crucially, we identify the precise conditions under which their coefficients ensure rational potentials, thereby enabling the explicit formulation of the corresponding Schrödinger equations and their solutions. Finally, we examine the link between these potentials and the shape-invariant property by analyzing the evolution of their supersymmetric partner potentials. These findings facilitate potential extensions to polynomials with cubic asymptotic behavior and explore the relationship among 1D, 2D, and 3D shape-invariant potentials within the context of 1D susy quantum mechanics. This work contributes to the broader understanding of special functions, their associated energies and eigenfunctions, and the dynamics of related 2D and 3D susy quantum systems. We construct a dynamic framework for distributing such opportunities within a society characterized by mobility bottlenecks, where optimal allocation involves balancing the immediate benefits to the current generation against the potential to uplift future generations' socioeconomic composition. Our analysis demonstrates that optimal allocations emerge from continuous optimization problems spanning multiple generations, revealing that these solutions often prioritize individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds over slightly more successful high-status peers—a form of affirmative action that arises organically from the pursuit of payoff maximization. Furthermore, we examine how model parameters influence whether this affirmative action is temporary or persistent, and we explore extensions incorporating more complex mechanisms governing transitions between socioeconomic levels. This research underscores how dynamic access models highlight the generational impacts of decision-makers' choices and the potential persistent generational effects of affirmative action policies. Access to university education serves as a potent driver of intergenerational mobility, allowing individuals to exceed the socioeconomic standing of their parents. We develop a dynamic model for allocating admission opportunities across generations that captures the tension between maximizing immediate payoffs and enhancing the socioeconomic composition of future generations. By solving optimal control problems optimized over two to three generations using empirical data from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, we illustrate how to calibrate the system dynamics portion of any access model. Our findings indicate that when designers optimize decisions over multiple generations, the resulting optimal access policies are forward-looking and resemble affirmative action, granting admission based on socioeconomic status rather than pure merit. These policies resemble quota-based systems because they emerge directly from the payoff structure without requiring explicit policy mandates. Furthermore, our analysis shows that various model specifications can yield significantly differing results regarding the persistence of these affirmative action-like behaviors. Additionally, we investigate extensions involving complex mechanisms governing socioeconomic transitions and access to elite institutions, demonstrating that persistent affirmative action can occur even in scenarios where one might expect rapid convergence to the socioeconomic status quo. Ultimately, this paper emphasizes how dynamic access models can reveal the potential persistent generational impacts of access decisions, particularly access to elite resources. Specifically, we show that when designers optimize university access over multiple generations, they may grant admission to less meritorious students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, a phenomenon that can persist across generations. In our specific numerical instance, every 1% increase in the university cohort from lower socioeconomic backgrounds reduces the societal Gini coefficient by 0.003 within three generations and by 0.006 in the long run. More generally, our findings suggest that persistent affirmative action can occur in a wide range of scenarios involving complex socioeconomic status determination mechanisms

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel rapid luminosity separation technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were executed systematically during every fill featuring full-intensity beams under physics production conditions at the Interaction Point (IP) of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment. This method enables the determination of both emittance and closed orbit parameters at the bunch-by-bunch level. By precisely measuring the beam-beam closed orbit discrepancies, researchers achieved a direct and quantitative observation of long-range beam-beam PACMAN effects, with results that align closely with numerical simulations generated by an enhanced version of the TRAIN code. Currently, data collected from these Emittance Scan runs at the LHC provide high-precision inputs for investigating short-range PACMAN effects within the fascinating regime of dynamic feedback stability. Furthermore, because Emittance Scans offer a precise and direct measurement of beam parameters, the technique is widely applicable in future high-power hadron facilities, which often operate under constraints regarding both emittance and closed orbit space at the interaction points.

background (CMB) serves as a fundamental probe in physical cosmology. Due to the faintness of this signal, researchers have developed increasingly sophisticated and sensitive experiments that observe the sky across multiple frequencies using thousands of polarization-sensitive detectors. However, the high sensitivity of these instruments means that instrumental systematic effects can become the primary obstacle to fully exploiting their data. This paper introduces s4cmb (Systematics for CMB), a Python package designed to simulate time-domain raw data streams from modern bolometric CMB experiments while injecting realistic instrumental systematics. The package aims to evaluate contamination from these effects in real data, inform the design of future instruments, and enhance the realism of simulated datasets necessary for developing precise data analysis techniques. s4cmb builds upon the e2sim simulation framework and was validated against the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and the Simons Array. Key features include the ability to rapidly evaluate the contamination level of K-band systematics in actual data—assessing both null tests and cross-spectral estimates—or to model experiments with future specifications, such as the Simons Observatory or the Cosmic Variance Limited (CVL) survey. These capabilities demonstrate that s4cmb can address questions regarding past, present, and future instruments. By providing a platform to address contamination issues in high-sensitivity observations, s4cmb paves the way for similar challenges in upcoming missions like CVL, the Simons Observatory, and CMB-S4. s4cmb is part of an open science initiative, encouraging other teams working on actual data to utilize it for their analyses. To facilitate this, we will gradually release systematics models specific to real experiments alongside our generic simulations. s4cmb represents a significant upgrade over our previous simulation tools, offering at least a 1000x speed increase over previous estimates of systematic contamination in ACT data. Furthermore, it represents a 10,000x speed increase over the necessary simulation times for evaluating these same effects in Simons Array data. The package is named after the Sanskrit deity of learning and wisdom, Shri Shanmukhamba (S4) cmb. The s4cmb package is released as open source, and we plan to share systematics models for actual data observations as they become available.

Abstract---Recent years have seen a surge in interest in generative models capable of creating photo-realistic forgeries of images and videos. These advances in deepfake technology enable the mass production of misinformation, posing significant risks to society. Consequently, accurate detection of deepfake media has become increasingly critical. This study introduces a novel approach combining contrastive learning with knowledge distillation to improve deepfake detection performance. By leveraging the knowledge embedded in deepfake images and videos, our method identifies regions with the highest deepfake artifact concentration. Numerical experiments and ablation studies confirm that the proposed method surpasses various state-of-the-art deepfake detection techniques. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AmirHosseinT/MD-CSDNetwork.

K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. First, we establish a novel inequality that extends the one found in references [9, 11] and provides a Busemann-Gromov type recognition criterion for conformal mappings between such spaces (Theorem \ref{main-thm}). Second, we derive a betweenness-relations-preserving version of Theorem 3.1 from [6] (Theorem \ref{thm-betweenness}). These results rely on a direct demonstration that a specific transformation of the angle function induces a betweenness relation on open intervals of real numbers (Theorem \ref{betweenness-by-thma}). We conclude with several comments linking our work to the research of A. Beauquier and F. Le Gall. New proofs are also offered for results by T. Iwaniec and J. Martin [7] and A. Beauquier [1]. Additionally, it is shown that a finding by G. David [4] follows directly from Theorem \ref{thm-betweenness}. Throughout the paper, computations are explicitly performed to illustrate how previously known findings emerge as corollaries of our main theorem.

For a number field $K$ of degree $n$ with embeddings $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$ into $\mathbb{C}$, the norm is defined as $\lvert x \rvert = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \lvert \sigma_i(x)\rvert^2}$ for any $x \in K$. Under this norm, an order $\mathcal{O}$ in such a field possesses successive minima satisfying $1 = \lambda_1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_n$. We investigate the metric discriminant $D_\mathcal{O} \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \lambda_i$ for orders $\mathcal{O}$ where $[\mathcal{O}: \mathbb{Z}]$ equals $n$ or $n-1$. It is demonstrated that $D_\mathcal{O} \geq n$, with equality holding if and only if $\mathcal{O} \cong \mathbb{Z} \oplies \dots \oplies \mathbb{Z}$ ($n$ times) or $\mathcal{O} \cong \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{1}] \oplus \dots \oplus \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{1}]$ ($n-1$ times). For the specific case of quadratic fields, we characterize orders $\mathcal{O}$ for which $D_\mathcal{O} \leq 2$. Furthermore, we provide precise counts of orders with a given metric discriminant for field degrees up to $20$. To our knowledge, this level of detail has not been previously documented for degrees exceeding $11$. Our findings extend to complex places and complex embeddings. Our proofs rely on reducing to lattices with specific symmetries and applying results from geometry of numbers, including weighted Minkowski bounds and successive minima on affine subspaces.

members of a hierarchical network are only profitable if a vast number of new participants continuously join; consequently, the absence of new recruits causes new entrants to lose their investments and forces existing members to withdraw funds. While these schemes are a global concern affecting diverse communities, their malicious intent is often obscured because participants can initially profit without actively defrauding others. This paper introduces a mathematical framework to elucidate the inherent deceptive nature of pyramid schemes, emphasizing how their reliance on endless new members ultimately leads to inevitable collapse and loss for the majority. Specifically, we clarify why distributing funds based on enrollment fees is mathematically unsustainable and how the necessary scale of new members required to profit exacerbates the deceptive impact. To demonstrate this phenomenon clearly and accessibly—even for non-specialists—we utilize a continuous approximation that employs exponential and logarithmic functions. Furthermore, we present a time-dependent model offering an intuitive explanation of the "rich get richer" dynamic, which is central to pyramid schemes. Although this model was originally designed to reveal the deceptive mechanics of illegal pyramid schemes, it can also be adapted to describe the community structure and information cascade dynamics observed in social media platforms like Reddit. However, we stress that such phenomena are not desirable in other online communities, as they can drive away existing, valuable members and foster misinformation cascades. Finally, we conclude by proposing regulatory measures aimed at mitigating the harmful effects of pyramid scheme dynamics in Reddit-like environments. The key contributions of this study are as follows: First, we demonstrate through a simple continuous model that the exponential growth necessary for upper-level members to profit in pyramid schemes is mathematically unsustainable and inevitably leads to scheme failure and widespread loss. Second, we provide a straightforward explanation of the "rich get richer" effect in time-dependent continuous models, illustrating how this dynamic is both inherent to illegal pyramid schemes and responsible for community structure formation and potential misinformation cascades in Reddit-like settings. Third, we suggest potential solutions to prevent illegal pyramid scheme dynamics in Reddit-like communities. Building on this foundation, we evaluate four Graph Neural Network (GNN) variants alongside a dropout-enhanced fully connected Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) to forecast the next activity's nature and timestamp. Unlike prior studies, we assess model efficacy across various process stages, segmented by quartiles of event counts and normalized case durations. This approach successfully located poles corresponding to RPA excited states, including the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. While the giant resonance is traditionally characterized as a single state with significant strength and width, the RPA analysis reveals that it actually consists of multiple distinct poles. The findings indicate that poles related to giant resonances are not singular but exhibit non-trivial distributions in the complex energy plane. In many of these contexts, the underlying systems are dynamic, and due to their inherent complexity, constructing mathematical models suitable for clustering is often unfeasible. This paper introduces a novel methodology for clustering dynamic systems based on their Lyapunov exponents, which serve as indicators of the system's underlying dynamics. Lyapunov exponent time series are demonstrated to yield clustering outcomes that are both qualitatively and quantitatively consistent with clustering strategies derived from financial time series features, such as the R/S statistic and volatility. When applied to dynamic systems spanning diverse domains—ranging from dynamic Monte Carlo simulations to actual data in physics, engineering, and economics—the proposed method consistently yields clustering results that are congruent with those of established techniques. These findings suggest that, given the right data, Lyapunov exponent time series are a effective tool for community detection. As a practical resource for researchers in diverse fields, the code used to compute the dynamic systems' behavior and perform the clustering is openly available online.

A potential advantage of mechanistic modeling lies in its capacity to integrate state-space frameworks, which assist in estimating unobserved physiological states and enhancing estimates of environmental state variables. This study introduces a population-level mechanistic model for red deer (*Cervus elaphus*) that jointly addresses individual location selection, physiology (body mass), and calving decisions. The model's key innovation involves representing the selection process as a function of threshold calving rules, which enable us to estimate rule distributions from observed calving data. We evaluated the model across two spatial scales using Scottish red deer data and compared its performance against alternative approaches by assessing estimates of physiological and calving traits, as well as the residual covariance between location and calving processes. Results indicate that a hierarchical structure capturing multiple biological scales yields superior performance compared to treating resource selection as an external input. Furthermore, the model demonstrated strong results when applied to both small herds and a large, managed population. Notably, in the larger population, the model revealed that while red deer spend approximately 50% of their time within 1.5 standard deviations of the calibration intensity (tree cutting), calving occurs almost exclusively outside this high-disturbance area. However, our analysis of the large population suffered from low within-individual variation due to seasonal grazing management and lack of movement variation among individuals during winter. Consequently, we propose applying this model to populations where calving rules are not uniform, where estimating non-spatial physiological states benefits predictions of calving location, and where investigating the scaling of resource selection from individual to population levels is of research interest. Ultimately, the model's capability to simultaneously estimate multiple biological processes makes it valuable for exploring management strategies, particularly during sensitive periods like calving. Built upon a flexible foundation, the model can be readily adapted to other species and populations, potentially yielding insights into their specific management challenges. The accompanying R package, MechRSD, facilitates the application of this modeling approach.

Our geometric theory of testing serves as the specification for a testing environment, which functions as the final stage of a toolchain designed to assist professional developers, hobbyists, and computer science students. This environment features an automated algorithm that identifies errors within executed tests and guides their correction by displaying a stick diagram of causal execution chains on a screen. Users can navigate this diagram backward, similar to using a satnav to follow roads on a map, which highlights the specific locations in the code that require modification to eliminate the error. Furthermore, we have established a formal theory of reliability, demonstrating that test execution conveys information about the current post-execution state by reducing the set of potential error locations—a property we term the location filter effect. Based on this effect, our environment's automatic algorithm searches for tests that specifically target a particular location, thereby preserving execution cost while ensuring that executed tests cover all sites where the reported error occurred. We have implemented this environment to experimentally validate the theoretical hypotheses presented in this paper; the environment is also available online for use by others. Our work represents the inaugural application of formal method technologies to the field of testing.

Questions regarding the appropriate execution strategy for tests during debugging are inherently complex, as they depend heavily on the specific context, a factor our automatic algorithm addresses by optimizing execution cost. Execution cost comprises both the expenses associated with running the test suite and the impact of test failures on development progress, such as the time required to analyze causes and the risk of obscuring other bugs. While prior execution strategies (references 1, 2, 3) have attempted to lower this cost through various methods, including selective execution and order optimization, these approaches lack a unifying theoretical foundation and do not guarantee the preservation of execution cost. We operate within the full information model, wherein Byzantine nodes can forge messages, omit transmissions, or adopt any arbitrary state. Under the promise that good (honest) nodes form a jointly connected subgraph, we establish both lower and upper bounds for the counting task across three distinct networking assumptions. First, under the pull-based assumption, we demonstrate a stark separation in feasibility: counting is achievable for $n$ nodes with $f$ Byzantine actors only when $n \geq 6f + 3$ (lower bound) or $n \leq 4f + 6$ (upper bound). Second, introducing a push-based mechanism yields a significant improvement, narrowing the feasible range to $n \leq 2.5n + 10$. This reduction represents the first improvement over the longstanding $\mathcal{O}(n)$ limit. Notably, this approach is fully decentralized, requires no messages to be sent more than polynomially relative to the actual network size, and functions even when $n < 1$. This result is achievable provided good nodes are 2-hop connected, i.e., $n \leq 1.33f + 3$. This bound is also tight, as a lower bound of $n \geq 1.33f$ is proven for this specific connectivity requirement. This achievement is notable because it functions in sparse networks where Byzantine actors constitute nearly 40% of the population. We propose a novel approach rooted in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Unlike conventional methods that treat the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation for a specified mean curvature $K$, our method solves an algebraic equation for $K$ given a chosen conformal factor. Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites represent an emerging class of materials that display diverse properties driven by their intricate electronic band structures and magnetic ordering. However, reports on the anomalous Nernst effect and its magnitude within this specific class remain scarce, a limitation likely attributed to the experimental challenges in accurately determining the anomalous Nernst coefficient. In this study, we present experiments on the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN antiferromagnetic antiperovskite thin films. By utilizing the same sample and measurement geometry for both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects, we enable a direct comparison between these phenomena to precisely quantify the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. Furthermore, we rigorously assess the spatial distribution of the thermal gradient across the sample and employ finite element modeling to validate our experimental findings. While the local measurements reveal that the thermal gradient is predominantly diagonal relative to the antiferromagnetic structure of Mn$_3$NiN, we also detect a smaller gradient arising from magnetoelastic strain. We interpret the emergence of this additional gradient through the modulation of the band structure, which occurs due to the coexistence of antiferromagnetic ordering and the cubic crystal field in this antiperovskite class. Finally, we discuss the temperature-dependent behavior of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN, as well as estimate the Seebeck coefficient for this material.

iller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, known as electro-elasticity, has been primarily investigated through the lens of piezoelectricity and piezoresistivity, with applications spanning damage detection to adaptive control systems like morphing aircraft. This article provides a comprehensive and integrated examination of the electro-elastic behavior of nanofiller-composites, drawing insights from both linear elastic dam-free conditions and the more intricate scenarios involving cracks, interfaces, and obstacles. These assessments utilize various nanofillers, with carbon nanotubes (CNTs) serving as the primary focus. By deriving analytical solutions and employing numerical methods, this study offers a thorough understanding of the nonlinear evolution of electrical conductivity, a critical factor for designing self-sensing composites. Furthermore, these findings facilitate the development of inverse problems aimed at estimating damage levels within such materials. The presented insights into the mechanical and electrical responses of nanofiller-composites deliver vital design principles for advancing self-sensing and self-healing composites. Consequently, these principles can facilitate the creation of advanced smart systems, including self-sensing bridges and damage-adaptive morphing aircraft. To support these advancements, this work compiles fundamental formulas and principles essential for researching nanofiller-composites and designing next-generation self-sensing and self-healing composites. Additionally, it highlights current challenges and potential future research trajectories within this field. The findings presented here are equally pertinent to nanofiller-composites reinforced with other micro- and nano-scale particulates, such as nanospheres and nanoplates. Crucially, the presented principles are universally applicable to self-sensing composites comprising any random distribution of conductive nanofillers embedded in a polymer matrix. Dynamic graphs are crucial for modeling phenomena across various domains, yet current classification methods often overlook the reality that node linking structures evolve over time. This study examines a classification task where node embeddings are trained not only on node and edge features but also on the temporal shifts of citation frequencies within dynamic citation networks. In this study, we investigate the topological and localization characteristics of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model featuring spatially correlated random binary disorder. Our findings reveal that such binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter regimes. These topological Anderson insulators are identified by a disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states, observable via the inverse participation ratio in both real and momentum spaces. Furthermore, the boundaries of the topological phases align with analytical predictions derived from the self-consistent Born approximation and the localization length of zero-energy modes. We also examine the influence of bimodal probability distributions on these disorder-induced topological phases and demonstrate that topological signatures can be detected through mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic setups. Ultimately, this work extends the concept of topological Anderson insulators to scenarios involving correlated disorders.

Predictions for the gluon-fusion channel rely on an explicit leading-order cross-section calculation for arbitrary complex parameters, enhanced by higher-order corrections: massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at NLO QCD, top-quark contributions up to N$^3$LO QCD within the heavy top-quark effective theory (including a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs component), and contributions up to NNLO QCD for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component and heavy Higgs bosons. The analysis also incorporates two-loop electroweak corrections in the heavy top-quark effective theory for light Higgs production and includes finite-width effects. Non-gluon-fusion channels are treated at LO QCD. For predictions involving the MSSM with complex parameters, both the explicit NLO QCD result and a result based on the probability distribution of the top-quark mass are provided; the latter offers an unbiased estimate suitable for any specific parameter point. Additionally, efficient Monte Carlo event generators implementing these physics processes are introduced. These generators utilize the explicit LO calculation for MSSM with complex parameters as a foundation and incorporate all aforementioned higher-order corrections via the provided Python code. The authors hope these predictions and computational tools will prove valuable in assessing the discovery potential of neutral Higgs bosons at the High-Luminosity LHC. The implementation for MSSM with complex parameters serves as a benchmark for similar calculations in other supersymmetric or non-supersymmetric models. Beyond the standard light Higgs, the implementation covers all other neutral Higgs bosons, including the heavy CP-even and CP-odd Higgs bosons ($H$ and $A$), as well as $H/A \to t\bar{t}$ production for various kinematic variables. Furthermore, the code facilitates the determination of branching ratios and production cross sections for all possible final states arising from Higgs boson decays.

The study examines the general elastic scattering process $M\gamma \to M$ for mesons $M$ composed of two quarks with different flavors. To our knowledge, this specific formulation of the contact interaction model alongside its application to elastic form factors and radius calculations has not been previously reported. The necessary theoretical frameworks and technical methodologies are universally applicable to other interactions and meson systems, offering significant potential for future research. The core idea involves treating a meson as quark-antiquark annihilating and recreating at a vertex, where an exchanged gluon generates a quark contact interaction. This mechanism yields the model's parameters by successfully describing the meson mass spectrum. Consequently, the contact interaction effectively encapsulates non-perturbative effects, including confinement, as well as the complex QCD dynamics of meson formation and decay. Elucidating the internal structure of hadrons remains a central objective of current experimental programs at facilities such as Jefferson Lab, Fermilab, and CERN. The emergence of the World Wide Web has accelerated the production and dissemination of news, simultaneously creating a challenge in helping users efficiently locate relevant current events. Automatic news topic modeling aids users in exploring popular and emerging events; however, current methods often lack the capacity to handle large-scale data or produce summaries rich in semantic detail. We address these limitations by developing a model named Eventus, which identifies news topics by representing them as event-specific eventhood distributions. Unlike prior work, the Eventus model is designed to identify emerging events and popular events within a world knowledge graph, offering summaries that include both constituent documents and associated news images. Experimental results on three datasets and a world knowledge graph show that Eventus identifies emerging events with an F1 score of 0.80 and popular events with an accuracy of 0.85. Implemented using vertex programming, Eventus processes world knowledge graphs containing up to 10 million nodes and edges. The source code is available at https://eventus-ml.github.io/.
