Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum of the annealing gap—can be identified through a dynamical quench parameter characterizing the post-quench quantum state. By integrating statistical methods, such as neural network training, with quench data, we can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap. We further show that insights gained regarding the annealing gap, either partially or fully, enable the design of optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical improvements in time-to-solution. These findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, which model challenging instances of the exact cover problem. Our results indicate that current-state-of-the-art annealing devices, such as those from D-Wave Systems, Inc., approach the limit dictated by the finite annealing time. Additionally, our optimized quench protocols and resulting annealing gaps are specifically designed for D-Wave hardware, showcasing significant time-to-solution improvements, including up to a factor of 20 for certain Hamiltonians. This enables us to determine the actual size of random Ising Hamiltonians solvable on existing machines. These findings are relevant to the community engaged in Ising Hamiltonian optimization and for designing efficient algorithms on future quantum computers. The accompanying C++ code is released open source.

two-band model for interface states in type-II Weyl and type-II nodal line semimetals captures the full three-dimensional many-body picture of these topological materials. By analyzing both the physical and mathematical sides, we demonstrate that these systems can be completely described by a set of two-dimensional effective parameters characterizing the Weyl or nodal line nodes within the Brillouin zone. This conclusion applies regardless of the complexity of the three-band nature found in specific crystals, such as CaAgAs. To support this, we provide explicit examples of such Weyl and nodal line semimetals, offering their respective effective parameters and mapping their complete three-dimensional magnetic responses directly onto these two-dimensional features. Finally, we generalize these findings to create a simple criterion for determining the 2D/3D nature of magnetic responses in any three-dimensional material. Our results imply that effective two-dimensional models can faithfully represent the intricate physics of three-dimensional magnetic responses in these systems, provided the spatial localization of Weyl or nodal line nodes and the properties of the effective surfaces in real space are properly accounted for. This insight facilitates a reduced dimensionality approach to engineering diverse 3D magnetic responses, including axial vector fields, by leveraging the mapping between effective 2D parameters and full 3D responses in these materials. This strategy can be extended to design complex magnetic responses, such as those found in anisotropic Weyl and nodal line systems. Our findings also hold significant importance for studying topological phase transitions between these states and for providing a general framework to understand the 2D/3D interplay in various magnetic responses across other topological materials. This approach may serve as a guide for exploring many other three-dimensional magnetic responses in existing and future materials. **Methods:** Our analysis relies on deriving the Hamiltonians and self-consistent fields for these metals using their effective two-band models, based on perturbation theory and the adiabatic approximation, respectively. We directly connect the 3D magnetic responses to the effective parameters and the 2D locations of the nodes in real space. Furthermore, we analytically and numerically demonstrate the equivalence between these effective two-band models and the original three-band models by showing they yield nearly identical magnetic responses. This confirms that the simpler two-band models faithfully capture the 3D many-body physics underlying these materials. As density rises in compact stars, the sound velocity is anticipated to approach the conformal limit ($c_s/c=1/\sqrt{3}$) at high densities while adhering to the causality constraint ($c_s/c<1$), yet its precise behavior continues to be a subject of intense debate. This study investigates the general characteristics of the sound velocity and adiabatic index across hybrid stars, neutron stars, and quark stars, employing various conditions for the hadron-quark phase transition with differing interface tensions. Our findings indicate that the anticipated sound velocity behavior can also arise from the nonperturbative properties of the quark phase, independent of a deconfinement transition, resulting in more compact stars with comparable masses. Consequently, we introduce a novel class of quark star equations of state that could be validated by future high-precision radius measurements of pulsar-like objects. Specifically, the parameter $\Omega=\int_0^\infty c_s(x) x n(x) dn(x)$, which quantifies the general nature of the sound velocity, can function as an effective critical density for the hadron-quark phase transition. We demonstrate that the minimum average quadrature uncertainty of these states can consistently fall below the standard quantum limit for sensing external fields. The states' non-classical characteristics are strongly influenced by the displacement parameter. Recent research has explored how the magnetorotational instability (MRI), the primary driver of disk viscosity, influences the VSI by examining magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence under stratified shear conditions. This study advances those efforts by investigating how thermal instabilities interact with VSI-developing MHD turbulence. Our findings indicate that when radiative cooling is active, the resulting two-dimensional (2D) structures can either amplify or suppress the VSI, a outcome determined by the specific characteristics of those 2D structures. Furthermore, these results are contingent upon the initial magnetic field configuration. Notably, in disks starting with vertical or weakly inclined large-scale magnetic fields, the MRI is triggered, causing MHD turbulence that either intensifies or mitigates the VSI. Conversely, disks initialized with diagonal large-scale magnetic fields experience an MRI that either promotes or hinders Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) development. While the MRI can create 2D structures capable of driving KHI, it can also generate current sheets and magnetic reconnection events that promote cooling and stabilize the flow against KHI. Overall, our study underscores the complexity of determining local disk viscosity arising from these interacting instabilities. These results have significant implications for theories regarding the formation of accretion disks, cooling mechanisms, and planet formation in protoplanetary environments. Future work will address the effects of three-dimensional (3D) radiative cooling on these instabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/soheih2001/thermal_VSI.

Since its discovery over three decades ago, the MRI has been established as the mechanism responsible for the viscosity observed in astrophysical disks. However, the operation of the MRI relies on the presence of a magnetic field, which necessitates an explanation for its origin. One such mechanism is the ambipolar electric current instability (ACI), a vertical instability arising from the differential motion between neutral particles and charged species in molecular gas disks. This study utilizes local, shearing-box simulations to assess whether ACI can generate the magnetic field strength required to activate the MRI. We conducted simulations varying the initial large-scale magnetic field orientation, the Toomre parameter ($Q$), and the mass ratio between neutral and ionized components. Our results show that ACI can indeed amplify an initially weak, external large-scale magnetic field to levels sufficient to trigger the MRI. These findings hold true for both epicy

We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. Furthermore, we show that any harmonic function growing at most polynomially decomposes into a sum of homogeneous harmonic functions, provided the scalar curvature is strictly positive everywhere except possibly at isolated points. Finally, considering three-dimensional Einstein manifons that are diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3$, we derive that the metric is conformally equivalent to the quotient of the standard sphere metric by a one-parameter isometry group; additionally, if the manifold is not diffeomorphic to the 3-sphere $S^3$, the metric is flat. This result offers a novel approach to a finding originally established by Cabezas-Apuntes and Cabezas-Rivas.

Among these, the data poisoning attack stands out as both highly impactful and increasingly difficult to detect and mitigate. In this study, we present TranspoSeD, a novel and potent data poisoning attack designed for neural network federated learning. This approach enables a malicious agent to stealthily inject its trained models into the aggregation process within a federated setup. Among these deviations, the parameter $\gamma$ significantly influences astrometric observations. This study investigates how theoretical gravity models map onto the PPN framework and assesses observational constraints on $\gamma$ using data from Gaia DR2 and Kepler. While DR2 alone yields limited constraints, combining it with Kepler's radial velocity measurements improves precision by an factor of four. The final estimate of $\gamma$ demonstrates strong robustness against variations in PPN parameters $\beta$ and $\xi_\gamma$, as well as against the specific implementation of gravitational redshift effects on spectral data. Furthermore, certain spectral classification systems introduce biases that must be accounted for to ensure accuracy. Ultimately, this approach offers a straightforward method to detect non-standard physics; any future detection of a $\gamma$ value differing from unity would signify a major breakthrough in our understanding of gravity.

To address this, we introduce a modular internal knowledge graph constructed within the model to enhance question answering. Our experiments on two distinct benchmarks demonstrate that adding relevant external knowledge to this internal structure improves answers, whereas including unrelated knowledge degrades performance. Furthermore, we release our dataset, model, and knowledge graph to help others investigate effective knowledge integration. Our results indicate that a model's ability to incorporate external knowledge depends on how well the knowledge aligns with the model's internal pre-trained knowledge and on the specific architecture and hyperparameters used. Overall, our approach offers practical insights and serves as a foundation for improving question answering through external knowledge.

Artificial Intelligence research increasingly utilizes external knowledge sources to enhance complex reasoning, but there is no consensus on the optimal method for incorporating this data. In this paper, we evaluate the inclusion of external knowledge in linear natural language forms versus structured knowledge graphs across two benchmarks. Our findings show that modern models struggle to access and integrate external knowledge, even when retrieval is guided by a parser. We propose leveraging the structured format of knowledge graphs and introduce a simple module for embedding relevant knowledge. Our experimental results indicate that this approach successfully integrates external information to improve question answering performance. However, we also discover that "noise" from non-target knowledge graphs remains a significant challenge. Ultimately, our work offers a framework for researching external knowledge inclusion and provides insights into designing effective systems. Our code and results are available at: https://github.com/jianyixw/noise-ekg.

Integrating external knowledge into language models has become a popular method for enhancing complex reasoning, particularly in question answering. However, most existing approaches retrieve knowledge in natural language, which can lead to noise and misinformation. This paper proposes using a structured knowledge graph format and a new embedding strategy to reduce noise and improve performance. Our experiments across two question answering benchmarks confirm the method's effectiveness. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the model's retrieval mechanism and the relevance of embedded knowledge are critical factors. Overall, our method offers a practical solution for incorporating external knowledge and provides insights for future research. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jianyixx/noise-ekg.

These cations generally exhibit brighter electronic emissions at longer wavelengths compared to their neutral counterparts. A comprehensive grasp of their near-UV to visible characteristics would enable their use as probes for local plasma conditions or as tracers for neutral gas within cometary systems. However, constructing complete spectral models for small, oxygen-containing molecular cations remains unfeasible due to current limitations in available molecular data. While the five simplest species—H₂O⁺, CO₂⁺, CO⁺, OH⁺, and O₂⁺—are well-characterized in certain spectral regions, they lack robust reference data in others. These knowledge gaps impede the creation of fully quantitative models of cometary spectra, specifically hindering accurate assessments of physical-chemical processes derived from the most prevalent cometary molecules. This work compiles existing spectral data for these species and identifies critical areas requiring future research, particularly where data scarcity significantly limits our understanding of cometary evolution. By aggregating current resources, we aim to assist experimentalists in efficiently utilizing cometary spectra and efficiently prioritize future investigations. Additionally, we emphasize the necessity of expanding beyond the current library of reference species to include more complex ions for effective cometary analysis. Ultimately, we advocate for the establishment of a coordinated program dedicated to improving molecular data quality through both ground-based and space-based experimental efforts.

justice system. Drawing on North Carolina court data from 1994 to 2009, this study assesses whether mandating mental health treatment as a condition of probation reduces the probability of future re-offending. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis compares probationers ordered to undergo treatment against those who were not. The findings indicate that requiring treatment lowers the three-year recidivism rate by 5.6 percentage points, representing a 17 percent reduction. The impact is strongest in preventing future violent and property crimes, with effects intensifying over time following conviction. Furthermore, a cost-benefit analysis demonstrates that the reduction in crime generated by the treatment exceeds the expenses associated with providing it. This metric captures the variety of local atomic arrangements as a continuous scale ranging from solid to liquid phases, defined relative to a distribution of thermal fluctuations. We demonstrate this new approach across three representative cases with differing degrees of disorder: (1) solid-liquid interfaces, (2) polycrystalline microstructures, and (3) grain boundaries. Using elemental aluminum as an example, we illustrate how our framework can monitor the spatio-temporal development of interfaces, including a mathematically rigorous definition of the spatial boundary between order and disorder. Additionally, we show how to derive physics-consistent gradients from these continuous disorder fields to aid in understanding and predicting material behavior and failure. Ultimately, our framework offers an intuitive and broadly applicable method for quantifying the link between intricate local atomic structures and macroscopic material phenomena.

While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. First, existing data preprocessing steps are often proprietary and custom-tailored, hindering experimental standardization. Second, current DLKT studies frequently employ inconsistent evaluation protocols that lack alignment with real-world educational settings. To resolve these issues, we present \textsc{pyKT}, a comprehensive Python-based benchmark platform designed to ensure valid comparisons across DLKT methods through exhaustive evaluations. The \textsc{pyKT} library features standardized, integrated preprocessing procedures for seven popular datasets across various domains, along with implementations of ten frequently compared DLKT models to facilitate transparent experimentation. Our rigorous, fine-grained empirical studies reveal key insights for effective DLKT, such as how incorrect evaluation settings can cause label leakage and artificially inflate performance, and how many recent DLKT improvements are marginal compared to the initial model by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have open-sourced both \textsc{pyKT} and our experimental findings at https://pykt.org/, and we invite contributions from other research groups and practitioners.

SMT solver veriT was introduced a decade ago at the inaugural PxTP workshop. Since that time, the format has evolved significantly. veriT proofs are now employed in various applications, and other solvers also produce proofs using this standard. To inform future enhancements, we seek community feedback. In this process, we examine the format's history, outline our pragmatic development strategy, and address potential issues that may emerge when other solvers utilize the format. We hope this analysis provides guidance for others interested in using or extending the format, and we welcome your comments. The format is openly accessible at https://github.com/veriT/veriT-proof-format.

Proof objects serve as a means to demonstrate the soundness of solvers; if a prover generates a proof object, checkers can validate its correctness. Additionally, they function as interoperable data structures within solving ecosystems. For veriT, these objects enable the analysis of intermediate steps during computation. We developed the current format with a focus on a bottom-up, pragmatic approach, ensuring compatibility with other solvers and maintaining a balance between necessary complexity and ease of human and automated processing. This results in a rich, expressive format. While one could design an ideal format theoretically, this is challenging due to the diversity of proving techniques, which may require substantial interpretation by checkers. Although such an ideal format could be simpler, it risks lacking the structural clarity found in our current solution. Ultimately, the decision to adopt this richer format was driven by its historical usage and its capacity to facilitate the creation of checkers with varying levels of sophistication. This post elaborates on these points and our rationale, providing background information that may assist others in developing their own proof checkers. The format remains available at https://github.com/veriT/veriT-proof-format.

We begin by providing an overview of proof techniques supported by veriT, illustrating how the format is utilized in these contexts. This includes a detailed explanation of the syntax and semantics, followed by a discussion of potential challenges arising from format misuse. Finally, we summarize our conclusions.

veriT employs several proof strategies, each with distinct characteristics. One approach involves deeply specialized algorithms where correctness is guaranteed by a specific correctness proof, and the proof object is straightforward because it maps directly to that proof. Conversely, hybrid approaches combine specialized algorithms with decision procedures for larger subterms, where correctness relies on the correctness of those procedures. Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Specifically, the final WER increased by only 2.2% (from 14.1% to 16.3%) when training on a model pre-adapted to Czech without accents, compared to a 9.6% increase (to 18.7%) when training directly on English. Additionally, we observed similar efficacy when the intermediate alphabet was German rather than Czech. These findings suggest that structurally related alphabets are more critical than linguistic similarity in end-to-end neural ASR. We release our code and models to facilitate future research.

To facilitate online predictions, we propose a sparse approximation that offers superior quality compared to existing rejection-based techniques. among strategic agents with additive valuations, assuming no monetary transfers. In this context, a mechanism is an algorithm that processes agents' reported valuations rather than their true ones. Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the allocated items. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), ultimately providing a comprehensive characterization of mechanisms capable of always reaching a pure Nash equilibrium. Notably, we develop novel algorithms to assign items that are EFX1—meaning one agent can take away any single good and the remaining allocations remain EFX1—and we demonstrate strategies for manipulating reports to induce equilibria in scenarios where pure Nash equilibria do not naturally exist. Our contributions include: showing in Section 3 that equilibria always exist when agents have cardinally comparable valuations (an outcome previously established by [15]); proving in Section 4 that both EF1 and EFX allocations are achievable regardless of agents' valuations; and in Sections 5 and 6, characterizing mechanisms for which pure Nash equilibria exist in all cases, noting that this characterization implies the equilibrium report equals true value for each agent (a result first introduced by [29]) alongside the achievability of EF1 and EFX allocations. We further explore prior literature on this topic and related fairness concepts in our Section 7. Our findings contribute to the understanding of designing mechanisms that prioritize equitable division of indivisible items.

Additionally, we propose novel quark current combinations and examine their correlations to explore intrinsic properties of the pion, such as its anomalous magnetic moment. These measurements can be executed with current lattice QCD computational resources and would enhance our comprehension of quark-level interactions driving the internal structure of hadrons.

analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, it requires accounting for varying observational conditions, such as distinct sample properties and data obtained from different methods. Although several studies have examined accretion rate distributions across the full range of disk masses, evidence for distinct populations remains inconclusive, often relying on assumptions that may not hold. By investigating the intrinsic scatter in the relationship between the X-ray and optical accretion rates derived from *Chandra* and *HST* observations of the T Tauri cluster V883 Ori, and comparing findings with other samples, we identify a sub-sample of objects exhibiting significantly lower mass accretion rates. This indicates the presence of a under-sampled low-accretion rate population, which may have been overlooked in prior analyses. We estimate that approximately 25% of T Tauri stars likely belong to this group. The scatter in the X-ray to optical accretion rate distribution can be explained by a combination of low mass transfer efficiency and a power-law structure for the boundary layer emission. However, the existence of this low-accretion rate population contradicts the standard viscous disk evolution model for T Tauri stars, even when initialized with the maximum observed masses in protostellar outflows. Consequently, external factors influencing the accretion of disk material must be considered to better understand the evolution of these systems. Potential causes for lower mass accretion rates include lower initial masses, mass depletion due to protoplanetary bodies, or mass ejection events like protoplanetary outflows or jet-driven eruptions. The distinct optical properties of this population, including lower mass accretion rates, softer X-ray spectra, and color excesses comparable to those from dust outflows, strongly support the hypothesis that a fraction of T Tauri stars is currently undergoing mass ejection. Future surveys combining multi-wavelength data will be essential to confirm this conclusion and elucidate the underlying mechanisms. The implied non-standard behavior of viscous accretion disks among a significant minority of T Tauri stars suggests that models of planet formation and evolution may require revisions.

This paper introduces a novel offline multi-agent policy learning approach that leverages such diverse data to discover interacting agents and synthesize their joint policies. conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal consequences of wave function collapse—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance." Decades later, Cleve adapted this same idea to design a localized nonlocal demonstration of quantum entanglement known as the CHSH game. In this game, two spatially separated players, lacking access to one another's inputs or outputs, strive to outperform classical limits in a task only feasible through quantum resources. This paper serves as a pedagogical exploration of the quantum CHSH game, intending to make the underlying physics and mathematics approachable for high school students and undergraduate students studying quantum information. Featuring numerous illustrations and step-by-step explanations, the work includes Python code examples designed to help readers grasp the core concepts of quantum nonlocality and appreciate the CHSH inequality's significance within quantum information theory. By elucidating how quantum entanglement enables players to bypass classical constraints, this exposition seeks to bring the excitement of current quantum nonlocality research applications to a broader audience. Additionally, it examines the connection between the CHSH game and the quantum Eraser experiment, reinforcing the counterintuitive reality that entangled particles can instantly influence each other across vast distances. Ultimately, this exposition provides an accessible entry point into the fields of quantum nonlocality, quantum entanglement, and quantum information theory.

advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations based on emerging IoV applications and data types. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of state-of-the-art privacy preservation techniques for IoV data, categorized into two groups: pan-specific and domain-specific methods. The survey begins by outlining the fundamental principles, characteristics, and privacy protection mechanisms associated with these approaches. Additionally, it examines the application of pan-specific privacy preservation strategies within the IoV context and identifies their limitations. Finally, the domain-specific techniques are explored in relation to key IoV applications, including location sharing, telemetry data transmission, image and video sharing, and license plate data analysis. Finally, upcoming challenges and potential research directions in this field are highlighted. This survey offers system architects and engineers a thorough understanding of privacy preservation mechanisms within IoV ecosystems and facilitates the development of more effective privacy protection strategies.

While prior gamma-ray data from Fermi and HESS during outburst provided only minimal insight, recent TeV measurements by the SWGO collaboration during quiescence offer significant details. The SWGO data indicate a power-law emission spectrum with a photon index of 2.3 ± 0.2 (stat) ± 0.5 (sys) for energies above 100 GeV, lacking a measurable high-energy cutoff. During outburst, the spectrum hardens, a behavior consistent with previous findings in other dwarf novae. By applying the hadronic model to fit the combined gamma-ray, X-ray, and radio emissions, we determined that the HESS observation during outburst aligns well with a hadronic origin, whereas the SWGO data from quiescence do not. Consequently, we conclude that the gamma-ray emission from V392 Per during quiescence cannot originate from proton-proton interactions within the standard accretion disk. Instead, we propose during outburst the source likely shifts toward a jet-dominated configuration, potentially producing gamma rays via electron-proton inverse Compton scattering. For quiescence, the emissions at X-ray and TeV energies probably arise from inverse Compton scattering by relativistic electrons within the corona. This scenario requires a sub-relativistic electron population (with a Lorentz factor of ~3) and an optical photon field with a flux approximately 10 times greater than typically observed. Furthermore, the absence of a gamma-ray cutoff in the SWGO results suggests the instrument's sensitivity may have influenced previous conclusions regarding the non-detection of cutoffs in other systems. Finally, comparing the derived magnetic field strengths across different models reveals that both the corona and jet scenarios demand fields significantly stronger than the critical field. These features may help distinguish between the structures and their potential particle-acceleration capabilities.

During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile terminal (MT) without transferring the codebook; the MT then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MT, as it relies on the observed signal to calculate the responsibility of each GMM component. Simulation results indicate that this proposed design and feedback scheme surpass conventional Lloyd clustering-based algorithms, particularly in scenarios with reduced pilot overhead. Furthermore, this approach offers a computationally efficient and straightforward method for designing capacity-achieving precoders with minimal feedback expenditure.

We present a framework to achieve these currents on a cubic three-dimensional (3D) lattice featuring a Hofstadter model connected to two heat baths at distinct temperatures. Our results demonstrate that these currents possess dissipative robustness, maintaining stability despite impurities and gauge field tilting within specific nonequilibrium states. Furthermore, we identify protected boundary currents with authentic 3D robustness, meaning their stability relies on tunnelling occurring across all three spatial dimensions. One-dimensional and surface currents exhibit similar robustness in both the integer and rational Landau gauge choices; however, the same is not true for bulk currents, which become trapped in localized states when these symmetries are spontaneously broken by the thermal gradient in the rational Landau gauge. investigate Population III (Pop III) binary remnant mergers within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) during the early stages of structure formation. We track the dynamical evolution of Pop III compact object binaries as they evolve through various galactic environments following their formation. Our findings indicate that while these binaries experience high stellar encounter rates, three-body interactions typically disrupt them before they can settle into nuclear regions. Specifically, gravitational three-body encounters are shown to efficiently eject one member of the binary at velocities ranging from 500 to 2000 km s$^{-1}$. These velocities are sufficient to propel Pop III black holes (BHs) beyond the escape velocity of ultramassive star clusters (~10$^{11}$ M$_{\odot}$) and massive galaxies (~10$^{12}$ M$_{\odot}$). Consequently, a substantial fraction of Pop III BHs is anticipated to reside in satellite substructures that will subsequently merge with larger galaxies. This mechanism could account observations of isolated massive galaxies lacking internal pop III star formation, as well as the unexpectedly high abundance of massive galaxies in the local universe. Furthermore, the capture and subsequent merger of these pop III BHs might contribute significantly to the observed population of supermassive black holes. Additionally, we calculate that the emission from these merging pop III BHs would peak in the gamma-ray spectrum, potentially being detectable by current and future gamma-ray telescopes. Consequently, capturing and merging pop III BHs emerges as a viable channel for constructing the population of supermassive BHs. This process also implies the in-situ creation of intermediate-mass BHs and ultramassive star clusters, which play crucial roles in galaxy evolution. These ultramassive clusters would subsequently drive long-duration feedback mechanisms, such as galaxy quenching and the assembly of central intermediate-mass BHs via the "missing link" scenario. Additionally, some ejected Pop III BHs might become trapped in the galactic halo, forming new dense clusters over cosmic time that could also contribute to the supermassive BH population. Ultimately, the detailed dynamics of early structure formation and the history of pop III star clusters are suggested to leave distinct imprints on the characteristics of central intermediate-mass BHs.关键词: galaxies: formation; black holes; stars: evolution; cosmology: early universe.

The proposed methods demonstrate significant improvements over existing literature, and simulation outcomes confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approaches across all proposed configurations.

However, their substantial model size hinders efficient inference and deployment, particularly on resource-constrained edge devices. To address this challenge, we introduce a model compression approach based on structured channel pruning and knowledge distillation, designed to significantly lower both the model size and parameter count of LSTMs while maintaining high accuracy. In an anti-de Sitter (AdS) setting, we demonstrate that the latter interpretation is incorrect; the conjecture fundamentally requires a specific mass-to-charge ratio. Consequently, this paper introduces the Electricity Sector Evolution Model (ESEM), a computational agent-based framework developed specifically for the long-run analysis of electricity investments and policy impacts in a diverse mix of power generation technologies and end-user types across various countries and regions. In this work, we consider a finite field $\F_q$ where $q$ is a power of a prime $p > 2$, and let $k = \overline{\F}_q$ denote its algebraic closure. We demonstrate that for any irreducible monic polynomial $f(t,x) \in k[t][x]$ of degree $n > 0$ which is separable over $k(t)$, the Galois group $\Gal(f)$ is generated by the Frobenius automorphism, implying that $\Gal(f)$ is cyclic. This leads to a classification of the Galois groups associated with monic polynomials in $k[t][x]$. Specifically, a finite group $G$ arises as $\Gal(f)$ if and only it is a finite quotient of the infinite wreath product $\Sym_\N \wrt \F_q$, thereby generalizing a finding by Odoni. spectroscopy to track the seasonal development and decay of large, warm vortices located poleward of approximately $75^\circ$ latitude in the stratosphere. Springtime thermal inversions heated the stratosphere to roughly $700$ K before collapsing into distinct vortex structures. While the poleward boundary of the main stratosphere was defined by the cold jet (marked by minimum zonal wind), the poleward boundary of the warm vortex relied on critical layer damping (CLD) of planetary waves (PWs) at upper stratospheric levels. While CLD effectively restricted the vortex boundary during the spring equinox, a more robust barrier was required to sustain the vortex through the summer solstice. During the final years of Cassini's mission, the northern hemisphere polar wind reached record-high magnitudes, exceeding $2000$ m/s in the northern polar region. This sustained high zonal wind generated a persistent jet that successfully maintained the warm vortex throughout the solstice. Consequently, the north polar region remained divided into three distinct thermal zones: the hot pole (above $80$ K), the warm vortex, and the cold summer night (below $70$ K) occupying the remainder of the northern hemisphere. These observations align with three-dimensional General Circulation Model (GCM) simulations of Cassini-era conditions, which indicate that sustained high zonal wind serves as the most efficient mechanism for isolating the polar region thermally. Notably, this contrasts with Earth's stratospheric dynamics, where sustained high zonal wind typically leads to polar cooling. On Saturn, planetary wave activity drives the breakdown of the jet and vortex formation; the resulting CLD activity determines the vortex's poleward extent. The intensity of PW activity during the final Cassini years was notably the strongest observed since the Pioneer and Voyager eras, accounting for the sustained high zonal wind in the northern polar region. However, the actual wind values surpassed GCM capabilities, as the model failed to generate sufficient PW activity to replicate the observed sustained high zonal wind in the north polar region.

mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity in the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^{d}$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the presence of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising in the second derivative of the variance that carry an unfavorable sign. To address this, our primary approach involves introducing a novel modified variance that is bounded from below and strictly concave for the specific solutions under consideration. Furthermore, we utilize the reflection principle to extend the existence and blow-up results to the case where the obstacle is the origin. These findings are significant because they extend the scope of variance-based blow-up analyses to problems involving obstacles and Dirichlet boundary conditions for the first time. Our methodology may potentially be extended to derive similar outcomes in the case of positive initial data across all dimensions for an obstacle located at the origin. By examining the underlying proof techniques, our contribution advances the comprehension of blow-up dynamics in Schrödinger equations with mass-subcritical power-nonlinearity when the obstacle is the origin, particularly regarding the influence of initial data characteristics on the nature of blow-up. The core components of our proof include the adaptation of the variance identity to accommodate obstacles, the development of the improved modified variance function, and the thorough characterization of solution behavior near the blow-up time.

to probe the molecular and atomic constituents of samples across diverse fields, including metrology, chemical analysis, and biological research. Despite the significance of these techniques, light-matter coupling strength in standard free-space setups is inherently limited, often necessitating long acquisition times and intense illumination that risks damaging sensitive materials. Light-matter coupling can be significantly enhanced by confining light within a local environment, particularly through nano-antenna structures based on metallic or dielectric antennas. These antennas act as transducers, converting free-space fields into concentrated near-field interactions at "hot spots," where an sample experiences fields orders of magnitude stronger than the free-space input. This document provides an overview of spectroscopic methods, the principles behind nano-antenna design, and current applications of scattering-type near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) in characterizing materials at hot spots. Additionally, we discuss emerging research applications, such as generating ultrafast optical fields at nano-antenna hot spots to probe chiral molecules and achieve enantioselective excitation. By leveraging these approaches, scientists can access significantly stronger optical fields to explore novel phenomena and effects unattainable with free-space fields, including circular-dichroism in single molecules and plasmon-enhanced Raman scattering. This technology also enables enantioselective excitation, allowing for the manipulation of molecular states based on their chirality.

applied to a new hybrid-dimensional model for single-phase Darcy flow in fractured porous media. The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed high-permeability fractures, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed low-permeability fractures. Consequently, the model supports both high- and low-permeability features essential for representing real-world geological media. Notably, across the entire domain, the numerical solution for pressure relies exclusively on the trace finite element space consisting of continuous conforming linear functions. However, the flux distribution is computed separately for the matrix and each fracture network, thereby avoiding inf-sup stability issues common in standard mixed finite element methods. Consequently, the solution exhibits a discontinuous flux across fracture–matrix interfaces but maintains continuous pressure. This approach allows for distinct numerical approximations of pressure and flux in both the matrix and fracture regions, offering significant advantages over existing methods that assume continuous pressure and discontinuous flux, particularly when high-permeability fractures are present. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Reproducible code is accessible at https://osf.io/y354c/.

Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. We also present analyses linking discourse markers with types of semantic and pragmatic relations between clauses, as well as their composite types regarding propositional attitudes. DiscSense serves as a valuable resource for researchers exploring theories of discourse structure and the cognition behind it, particularly by enabling the bottom-up investigation of relationships between discourse markers and discourse relations, a task currently unfeasible with automatic prediction due to the lack of annotated corpora. DiscSense was constructed using the model by Nguyen et al.~\cite{nguyen2019discourse}, and we describe our inference procedure, which involved sampling from posterior distributions using data from existing semantic classification datasets, followed by clustering to identify categories. DiscSense exhibits no overlap with the RST dataset~\cite{bergsma2019rst}. DiscSense encompasses a broader range of discourse marker types and relationships compared to resources like RST~\cite{prnls14}, yet it remains complementary, as it is predictive rather than generative. We hope DiscSense facilitates new research into theories of discourse structure, especially by aiding the bottom-up induction of annotations necessary for establishing relationships between markers and discourse relations. DiscSense reveals that markers clustering together prior to inference do not necessarily so afterward, both within and across different discourse marker families. Furthermore, certain markers do not exclusively express relationships of types previously attributed to them. DiscSense is also applicable to other languages, though this requires developing a suitable prediction model.

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (R1) a neighborhood around the target parameter where the objective is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (R2) areas surrounding all strict saddle points; and (R3) remaining regions characterized by large gradients. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that geodesic convexity holds in a neighborhood of local minimizers. Our proofs rely on a detailed landscape analysis of a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, serving as a pivotal intermediate step. Additionally, our conclusions rest on a standalone result identifying that the geodesic ball centered at $Y$ with a radius equal to one-third of $Y$'s least singular value forms a geodesically convex set under the Riemannian quotient geometry.

This finding appears to contradict the aforementioned conjecture only marginally, as the subclass's defining conditions are relatively intricate. Furthermore, we present an efficient polynomial-time algorithm to construct the strong edge-coloring for this specific class of graphs. These findings may hold significance for designing 5-dimensional local area networks (LANs) and 5-color code-division multiple-access (CDMA) networks, as the graphs under consideration model various physical network topologies. To our knowledge, this work achieves the first efficient strong edge-coloring for any family of graphs for which the existence of such colorings was previously unknown.

Extending beyond simple word alignment, we implement multiple cluster-level alignments, ensuring that word clusters maintain consistent distributions across different languages. Our clustering strategy leverages three distinct signals: (1) neighboring words within monolingual embeddings, (2) character-level data, and (3) linguistic properties (such as plural markers and negation prefixes) derived from linguistic knowledge graphs. We evaluate the quality of both vertex and cluster alignments using several automatic cross-lingual knowledge assessment metrics. Additionally, we introduce a novel evaluation method based the linguistic accuracy of translations for aligned pairs. Our results indicate that our proposed evaluations yield scores strongly correlated with existing knowledge assessment metrics, while also offering superior language pairing capabilities. Finally, our experiments demonstrate that even with sparse data in low-resource languages, our cluster alignments yield significantly more accurate machine translations compared to state-of-the-art methods that rely on vertex alignments alone. The our code is publicly available here.

Abstract: We present a method for estimating the accuracy of machine translations by leveraging linguistic knowledge graphs. Our approach assigns numerical scores to individual words and phrases based on the semantic distance between the predicted and reference translations. We compare our results against a range of baselines, including metrics based on n-gram overlap, string similarity, and a cross-lingual knowledge-based approach. Experiments conducted on English-to-other language pairs reveal that our method outperforms traditional evaluation metrics, especially in scenarios with sparse reference data. We perform experiments across 17 language pairs, encompassing both high- and low-resource languages. Our code is accessible at this link.

Abstract: This study introduces a novel evaluation method for machine translation that utilizes linguistic knowledge graphs. By assessing the semantic distance between predicted and reference translations at the word and phrase levels, our results overcome the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics. These metrics rely on extrinsic knowledge from native speakers and are especially effective in low-resource settings. Our findings show that this approach surpasses standard evaluation protocols. Experimental outcomes across 17 language pairs (including English-to-Swedish, German-to-Hungarian, and English-to-Korean) confirm that our method aligns closely with standard metrics and produces reference-free scores with high accuracy. Furthermore, the method is particularly advantageous for low-resource languages, yielding an 11.2% improvement over standard evaluation metrics in such contexts. Our code is available at this address.

Transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) spectra and integrated yields are derived across various centrality bins, ranging from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb collisions, characterized by final-state multiplicity. By examining both Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions, the study investigates systems with comparable charged-particle multiplicities but distinct initial geometrical eccentricities. A detailed comparison of spectral shapes between these two systems highlights an inverse relationship between radial and elliptic flow. Specifically, the results indicate that radial flow remains independent of the colliding system when normalized to similar charged-particle multiplicities. Regarding hadron chemistry, the previously noted smooth progression of particle ratios with multiplicity from small to large systems is also observed in Xe-Xe collisions. Furthermore, these findings confirm that two key characteristics of particle production at LHC energies apply to medium-sized nuclei: a proton-to-pion ratio lower than thermal model predictions and an increasing $\phi$-to-pion ratio as final-state multiplicity rises. Finally, the results reinforce the applicability of thermal dynamics to medium-nucleus collisions and suggest that hadron chemistry indications of quark gluon plasma formation in heavy-ion interactions are present already at LHC energies with small-nucleus collisions.

This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. These findings offer a quantitative perspective on the complex interplay between collective behavior and urban design during periods of civil disorder. The research underscores the utility of integrating key elements of population dynamics—such as mobility, density, and interaction—into mathematical frameworks to investigate the underlying causes of riots. Consequently, future investigations aiming to model past events or forecast future unrest must incorporate a population displacement mechanism to ensure a precise representation of the phenomenon. The methodology and findings presented here can serve as a foundation for studying similar phenomena in other major cities or smaller towns.

Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. . Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant attention because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes. Furthermore, ablation studies provide insights into the contribution of each component within our framework. Finally, we highlight the potential of using attention mechanisms for sensor fusion in learning-based VIO systems and offer suggestions for future research directions. Experimental validation was conducted using the TUM and RVB datasets.

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. The concept of square-root topology has been well-established in light waveguides and photonic platforms, yet its realization in 3D solid-state systems remains unexplored. This state manifests as Fermi-arc surface states and hinge states with a square-root dispersion relation. These phenomena were observed in a 3D stacked electric circuit consisting of honeycomb-kagome hybrid layers connected via double-helix linkages. Our work demonstrates that complex 3D structures can generate formidable square-root topology, providing a systematic approach to designing exotic square-root square-root square-root states in 3D solid-state architectures.

These results hold significant importance for inverse scattering issues involving obstacles with partially unknown boundaries. Additionally, the code has been enhanced to solve inverse problems for the Schrödinger equation with obstacles, yielding promising results. This enhancement relies on adapting a specific variational formulation of the QRM developed by the authors. Similar improvements can be applied to other inverse problems involving hyperbolic, parabolic, or evolution equations. The algorithm features low computational costs, exhibits robustness against measurement noise, and demonstrates high accuracy. The quasi-reversibility method is notably effective for ill-posed problems; however, boundary data completion for Maxwell fields was previously unresolved until now. While authors in [15, 16] tackled data completion for the scalar wave equation via boundary control and observability techniques, those methods are not applicable to vector fields such as the electric field. Additionally, existing literature lacks works on data completion for other evolution equations, including the Schrödinger, heat, and Navier--Stokes equations. Although various studies exist on inverse problems concerning obstacles with partially unknown boundaries for the Schrödinger equation—often relying on iterative methods like the boundary element method coupled with nonlinear optimization, adjoint states, or the shape calculus—the present research offers a superior alternative through its non-iterative nature. Although boundary data completion for the Schrödinger equation was previously solved non-iteratively by [35] using Tychonov regularization, that approach suffers from lower accuracy and higher computational costs compared to the QRM. FedSA), a novel knowledge-amalgamation problem aimed at training a student model for a specific new task using multiple decentralized teacher models. These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. Our motivation arises from a current challenge in model sharing: despite significant investments in training large, capable networks, researchers and institutions often cannot share their pre-trained models due to privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, even when they wish to contribute. FedSA addresses this dilemma by enabling the creation of a specialized student model for a task different from any of the teachers' original domains. To achieve this, we propose a dedicated strategy where the student training process employs a new saliency-based method to adaptively select participating teachers and integrate their key capabilities. We evaluate FedSA's performance across both single-task and multi-task scenarios. The experimental results confirm that FedSA effectively amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models, achieving results comparable to centralized approaches that utilize teachers with identical or superior capabilities. Furthermore, experimental analysis reveals that replacing our selection mechanism with other methods leads to performance degradation, demonstrating that FedSA comprehensively solves the decentralized knowledge amalgamation problem. To our knowledge, this is the first solution allowing for the training of a student model for a novel task through decentralized teachers with unknown and dissimilar domains. Additionally, our approach offers a unified framework for knowledge amalgamation that accommodates both similar and dissimilar teacher capabilities. The source code is available at https://github.com/ZiyangLu1999/FedSA.

Abstract: Deep learning models trained on private data can often achieve comparable performance to those trained on data from diverse sources. This paper introduces a new, cost-effective approach for transferring knowledge from a student network to a teacher network with superior performance. First, we identify the task discrepancy between the student and teacher by calculating the difference in their loss functions. We then selectively update the student's parameters by incorporating the gap-specific knowledge from the teacher's update rules. This allows the student to acquire novel information unique to the teacher's domain without overfitting. Experimental results on image classification and speech recognition show that our method effectively transfers knowledge from teachers with both similar and dissimilar capabilities, outperforming existing state-of-the-art knowledge distillation techniques. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuxia/SDKD.

Assuming $\mathrm{rk}(E/\mathbb{Q}) \leq 1$ and imposing additional constraints on $E$, we demonstrate that there exist infinitely many $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank does not increase, meaning $\mathrm{rk}(E/K) - \mathrm{rk}(E/\mathbb{Q}) = 0$. Our approach involves controlling the 2-Selmer rank of $E$ within specific quadratic extensions, a method that also applies to $A_4$ quartic fields. These findings align with a broader conjecture by Skinner and Urban regarding the typical rank behavior of elliptic curves across families of number fields. To achieve this control, we calculate the Hilbert Symbol of defining polynomials associated with quadratic extensions, a process that requires determining the Legendre symbol of special values of the Dedekind zeta function of the quartic field modulo $2$. Our computations rely on algorithms by Schoof and Schoof and Schoof and Stein. While previous studies have addressed rank non-decrease in quadratic extensions using class field theory and Iwasawa theory, our work is distinctive in employing the Cheisnokhman-Gross-Konno-Mizumoto formula for the Hilbert Symbol derived from the residue of the Dedekind zeta function. As an application, we provide explicit examples of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions whose rank equals that of the base field $\mathbb{Q}$. A key innovation of this paper is a general algorithm for computing the Hilbert Symbol mod $2$ via the Residue of the Dedekind zeta function, applicable to any prime and degree, which may prove useful in related mathematical areas. To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible heat transformation into work in one-dimensional interacting lattice models. By examining specific examples of lattice models with local Hamiltonians—both in the ground state and thermal states within the long-wavelength limit or theoretical limits—we find that the QNEC does not generally mandate the unidirectional flow of heat from hotter to colder regions when a local operation converts heat to work. However, we also demonstrate that an infinitesimal irreversible heat flow from colder to hotter regions violates the QNEC. These findings indicate that, in one-dimensional lattice models, the QNEC solely limits the magnitude of the otherwise unconstrained microscopic reversal of the classical heat law. These results are entirely based on lattice models with local Hamiltonians in one dimension, do not rely on geometric assumptions about spacetime dimensionality or curvature, and involve no approximations regarding the state's complexity. Consequently, our conclusions robustly affirm the necessity of the irreversible heat flow from colder to hotter regions in the context of quantum nonequilibrium thermodynamics and strengthen the physical foundations of the second law of thermodynamics through the QNEC. This study does not depend on any assumptions concerning the spacetime geometry, dimensionality, or curvature. Specifically, when analyzing local Hamiltonian lattice models with local Hamiltonians under the same conditions as the examples in this paper, it becomes evident that the QNEC only restricts the small-scale (microscopic) violation of the conventional heat flow direction. Thus, our results reinforce the physical validity of the second law of thermodynamics within the framework of the quantum null energy condition while providing a clearer picture of heat-to-work conversion in one-dimensional lattice models. Crucially, this work involves no continuum approximations and remains applicable to any complexity of the lattice state. These findings robustly support the understanding of irreversible heat flow from hotter to colder regions in quantum nonequilibrium thermodynamics and firmly ground the second law of thermodynamics via the QNEC, particularly for lattice models where spatial curvature effects are negligible. Ultimately, our analysis confirms that the second law of thermodynamics, when refined by the QNEC, does not prohibit—but merely constrains—the microscopic reversal of heat flow in lattice models, as the entanglement entropy of any subsystem strictly adheres to the null energy condition. We denote by $\Pi_1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ the set of polynomials of degree at most 1, which corresponds to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Consider the interpolation projector $P: C(Q_n) \to \Pi_1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ defined by $n+1$ nodes $x^{(j)} \in Q_n$ such that $Pf(x^{(j)}) = f(x^{(j)})$ for $j=1, \dots, n+1$. Let $\|P\|_{Q_n}$ denote the operator norm of $P$ mapping $C(Q_n)$ to itself. When $n+1$ is an Hadamard number, a nondegenerate regular simplex with vertices located at the corners of $Q_n$ exists. This text demonstrates that for any configuration of nodes $t = \{x^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{n+1} \subset Q_n$, the norm of the associated projector satisfies $\|P_t\|_{Q_n} \geq \sqrt{n+1}$, which implies that the minimal norm is attained precisely by a regular simplex. Consequently, the regular simplex is characterized as the unique node distribution that minimizes the norm of the interpolation projector onto affine functions over the unit cube. This result extends a finding by V. A. Yudin, who established that $\|P\|_{Q_n} \geq \|P\|_{Q_2} = \sqrt{3}$ for all $n \geq 2$. As a corollary, we observe that $\|I-K_P\|_{C(Q_n)} \geq 1 - \|P\|_{Q_n} \geq 1 - \sqrt{n+1}$, where $I$ is the identity operator and $K_P$ is the linear operator projecting differentiable functions to their best approximation in the uniform norm by a polynomial of degree 1 on $Q_n$. Therefore, the existence and uniqueness of such a projection remain an open problem.

In this study, we employ terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy (SNOM) to examine the local dielectric characteristics and carrier densities of wet-etched aluminum resonators on silicon, a fundamental component of superconducting quantum processors. Leveraging a newly developed vector calibration method, we derive THz permittivity from spectroscopy conducted near the microwave feedline. By fitting the extracted permittivity to the Drude model, we determine that silicon within the etched channel exhibits a higher carrier concentration compared to buffer oxide-etched silicon, and we investigate post-processing techniques to lower these levels. The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, spanning timescales from milliseconds to billions of years. These phenomena include volatile delivery and recycling via comets and asteroids, radiative and convective climate dynamics, tectonic and volcanic activity, crustal recycling, and magnetic field generation. While significant progress has been made in understanding the links between interior and exterior systems—such as connecting the core to the ionosphere and the mantle to the crust—many open questions persist. For instance, could a lack of crustal recycling impede the recirculation of carbon, thereby influencing the climate? Might the absence of an intrinsic magnetic field have impacted the atmosphere's history? Can geodynamic and climatic feedbacks generate chaotic behavior across different timescales? Modeling these feedbacks requires simulations that capture events ranging from meteorite impacts to cloud formation. Although current simulations successfully account for Venus's climate across various timescales, they rely on simplified representations of volcanic, tectonic, and crustal recycling activities. Capturing the atmosphere's evolution alongside realistic interior activity would require resolving phenomena from the core to the crust, a task beyond current computational capabilities. Instead, this work adopts a bottom-up approach to investigate potential feedbacks between the interior and atmosphere by combining models of core dynamics, mantle convection, crustal formation, and atmospheric evolution. These models simulate the emergence of a molten Venus over a 5 Gy timeframe, addressing the generation and evolution of the core's magnetic field, the tectonic and volcanic cycles governing crustal recycling, and the resulting climate feedbacks and volatile recycling cycles. Initial simulations indicate that a global stagnant-lid tectonic regime is most likely to produce feedbacks between the interior and atmosphere. However, when simulating the emergence of Venus without an intrinsic magnetic field, the simulations evolve a resurfacing mode characterized by volcanism, meteorite impacts, and volcanic glass formation that disrupts the atmosphere. Furthermore, a cycle emerges where the supercritical CO2 atmosphere controls the climate, driving reversals in the direction of mantle convection every 1–10 Gy. This recycling cycle causes periodic bursts of volcanism and meteorite impacts that strip portions of the atmosphere back into the crust and mantle. Identified as a rare Ca-rich supernova, SN~2020jfo emerged as a bright point source 9.6" off-center in the WFC3 camera on the Swift satellite. The progenitor was a sub-solar mass ($0.47 \pm 0.04 M_{\odot}$) carbon-oxygen white dwarf exhibiting significant surface contamination from helium and heavy elements, indicative of accretion from a non-degenerate companion within a close binary system. Compared to other Ca-rich supernovae, SN~2020jfo displays a notably rapid early evolution characterized by steep declines in both $V$-band magnitude and Ca II $\lambda$8600 absorption features during the first week post-explosion. Spectral analysis during this initial phase reveals strong absorption from Fe II and Ca II multiplets, alongside prominent blue-shifted features attributed to ejecta expanding against the white dwarf's gravity. By $\sim$5 days after explosion, the spectral characteristics began aligning with those typical of Ca-rich supernovae. Spectral modeling employing a radiative transfer approach indicates that the rapid post-explosion evolution is driven by the small size of the white dwarf and the low density of the surrounding circumstellar environment. Additionally, late-time infrared observations and spectral energy distributions suggest the presence of dust within the expanding ejecta, roughly 80 days after the event. The rapid brightness decline and spectral changes underscore the value of ground-based time-domain observations for uncovering the physics of these transients in future discoveries. SN~2020jfo expands our understanding of white dwarf explosions and aids in refining census efforts of these rare events. Given its early discovery and concentrated data collection, SN~2020jfo serves as an exemplary case of a Class Ia fast transients (Ia-CSTs) episode, potentially triggered by interactions with an accretion disk or a filling-factor companion. These fast Ia-CSTs are hypothesized to result from more rapid mass accretion scenarios than those characterizing standard Ca-rich supernovae. In this MuLE configuration, multiple lobster-eye modules observe different sky regions and merge their images electronically before sending data to a single detector. These results suggest that MuLE telescopes offer a highly efficient method for building wide-field X-ray observatories and serve as an excellent complement to focusing telescopes for multi-scale astronomy. For events involving neutron stars, the concurrent detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation offers significant potential to deepen our understanding of these phenomena and investigate the equation of state of dense matter. However, achieving electromagnetic detection demands that source signal strengths exceed the sensitivity thresholds of current instruments across the entire electromagnetic spectrum. Focusing on the gamma-ray domain, the most probable yet hardest to observe channel for NSBH mergers involves the gravitational wave emission and gamma-ray jets associated with relativistic outflows. This study focuses on estimating the sensitivity of future third-generation gravitational wave detectors and forthcoming generation-4 light detectors for NSBH events, while also projecting the observability of their gravitational wave and gamma-ray signals with upcoming gamma-ray telescopes. We further examine the physical factors influencing the detectability of these mergers in multi-messenger observations and how they factor into future search strategies. Our results indicate that third-generation GW detectors could potentially observe both gravitational waves and gamma rays from ~10,000 to 100,000 NSBH merger events annually, whereas current LIGO and Virgo facilities are limited to detecting approximately 20 such events per year based on gravitational waves alone. With favorable conditions, future gamma-ray observatories might detect up to 20,000 NSBH mergers per year. We have selected representative models for four typical NSBH merger scenarios and calculated their gravitational wave signal-to-noise ratios using next-generation detectors, along with their electromagnetic detectability via future gamma-ray instruments. These findings will assist in optimizing the parameters of actual NSBH merger models for future multi-messenger observations. Our conclusions suggest that the era of precise measurements for nearby NSBH mergers through combined gravitational wave and gamma-ray observations will commence with third-generation detectors and will be significantly advanced by future gamma-ray observatories. Ultimately, characterising the inner disc resolution, migration behaviour, and mass limits of forming companions is crucial for fully understanding HMYSOs and their feedback mechanisms. This paper explores the use of BERT for annotating dialogue acts in Twitter interactions, a process that can be broadly categorized into rule-based and rule-free approaches. In contrast, the rule-free method relies on a trained neural network to learn the mapping between linguistic features and dialogue act labels from annotated data (Liampotsis *et al* 2020). This paper introduces a novel representation and filter based on the most robust existing methods to upgrade the algorithm. The new version, named improveAlgo, surpasses moosAlgo's performance in unknown environments and matches the speed of state-of-the-art algorithms when the map is complete. Furthermore, improveAlgo utilizes a modern, high-performance C language, offering easier integration into various robotic platforms. Performance assessments were conducted in both virtual and physical unknown rooms, consistently showing improveAlgo outperforming other state-of-the-art algorithms. The improveAlgo source code is publicly accessible via GitHub.
