In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "searchlight" on the local field experienced by atoms—and a gravitationally accelerated drop of ferrofluid, which "traps" the local field, also affecting the atoms. By performing atomic interference experiments in the presence of these expelled and trapped magnetic fields, we can precisely quantify the field's trap and expulsion strengths, thereby deriving the magnitude of the local magnetic field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the strength of the expelled field can be calculated using only classical physics and measurable quantities, such as the de Broglie wavelength and the fringe position in the interference pattern. In contrast, deriving the trapped field requires the Dirac equation; we achieve this by computing the de Broglie wavelength and the position of the first maximum or minimum in the interference pattern, identifying this point as a Dirac node. We support these findings with numerical simulations of the Mach-Zehnder interferometry experiments. Because the searchlight and trap effects offer high sensitivity, the method's robustness can be significantly strengthened by conducting measurements at multiple positions around the superconductor and the ferrofluid drop, respectively. Ultimately, this approach provides a simple yet highly sensitive technique for detecting magnetic fields, requiring no prior calibration. This methodology can be generalized to measure the local magnetic field in front of any object.

Nevertheless, many developers instinctively code in OOP because it effectively models their domains. We investigated whether existing OOP languages could be adapted to exploit SIMD instruction set extensions for parallelism, specifically targeting STOMP (Single Instruction Multiple Data Object-Oriented Parallel Model), which was designed to maximize SIMD utility on objects and arrays. To address the complexity of manually writing high-level OOP code in a manner suitable for parallelization, we developed JAMP (Java Array-Mapping Parallelism), an approach that treats objects as arrays to enable straightforward SIMD implementation. JAMP represents objects within a type's family using a shared array, storing individual instance data in the array's lanes. Each thread processes multiple data points simultaneously via identical instructions operating on these lanes. To accommodate individual object variability, we encoded it into a mask and a compact key. This mask allows threads to execute instructions selectively across instances, while the key enables efficient, vectorized index-based hashing for hash table operations. We validated JAMP's performance through a suite of 20 standard Java library implementations. Additionally, we demonstrated its effectiveness with complex objects featuring nested structures and intricate hash table operations. Our findings indicate that JAMP achieves up to 120x speedup for specific benchmarks on modern CPUs with wide vector units, achieving a median speedup of 13.6x (IQR: 7.8--24.2), and consistently maintains within one order of magnitude of hand-optimized assembly code across all tests. Furthermore, we show that JAMP's design is domain-agnostic and can be readily extended to support new data types. JAMP source code and a repository of experimental results are publicly available at https://cs.uoregon.edu/~moir/jamp.

Through a detailed orbital decomposition of local densities of states, we examine the formation mechanisms of YSR states for an Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, contrasting our theoretical outcomes with recent experimental data. For the adatom, our findings indicate that spin-orbit coupling causes minor shifts in certain YSR peaks, while local spin-polarization on Nb atoms has negligible influence on their positions. Furthermore, scaling the exchange field at the Mn site accounts for the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum. Our results for a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer align well with the experimentally observed splitting of YSR states; however, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, the spin-orbit coupling proves insufficient to explain the experimentally observed splitting. Additionally, altering the relative orientation of magnetic moments within this dimer induces splitting and energy shifts of the YSR states, ultimately resulting in the emergence of a zero-bias peak for the deepest YSR state. Finally, we conclude that the energy splitting of YSR states in Kramers doublets arises from the exchange interaction, whereas the splitting among non-Kramers doublets is driven by the spin-orbit coupling. Overall, our computed spectra for both the Mn adatom and adatoms in dimels on Nb(110) show good agreement with recent STM experiments, reinforcing the conclusion that the discrete energy levels of YSR states can be precisely engineered to support both qubit operations and quantum gate protocols. Our methodology offers significant utility in interpreting recent STM/STS studies on YSR states and assessing the feasibility of utilizing YSR states as qubits on specific substrates.

This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{25}$ W/cm$^2$, positron generation enters a highly polarized quantum radiation pressure acceleration (QRPA) domain, where their polarization arises from spin-helicity coupling among laser photons radiated by positrons within the external QED critical field. Furthermore, we observe that positron polarization gradually shifts from linear to circular as intensity increases beyond $10^{26}$ W/cm^2, as circular polarization becomes energetically favorable in the quantum QRPA framework. These findings are validated by extensive particle-in-cell simulations that include particle spin and radiation reaction, contrasting with traditional models lacking radiative effects that fail to account for positron polarization. Finally, we discuss the significance of these discoveries for advancing laser-solid physics and potential applications in positron beam technology and beyond standard model QCD investigations.

In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes. These conclusions also imply that such groups satisfy a polynomial version of both the Collatz Conjecture and the weak Goldbach Conjecture. Furthermore, we establish a polynomial bound for the diameter of the symmetric group $S_N$ relative to the generating set $[N-1,2]$. Throughout the proof, we provide an explicit formula for the exact diameter, which we analyze for various values of $N$.

cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud (designated as G28.37+0.07 or G28.34+0.06) classifies them into protostellar and starless groups based on their connection to molecular outflows. Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. Consequently, massive star formation may not necessarily originate from massive prestellar cores, contingent upon the rate of this mass accretion. The implications of this finding for the relationship between the core mass function and the stellar initial mass function require further investigation. Additionally, the mass spectrum of protostellar cores in the Dragon IDL differs notably from that in the G28.37 molecular outflow cluster within the Orion complex. This suggests that core accretion rates are governed not solely by local conditions but also by the broader environment. As star formation progresses and the cluster density increases, accretion rates are expected to decline due to potential sources of mass depletion. Therefore, in regions where core accretion is primarily limited by available mass, the Dragon IDL is likely to yield a top-heavy stellar initial mass function. The Dragon IDL represents a later stage in cloud evolution compared to the G28.37 cluster; thus, to comprehensively understand the origin of massive stars, it is essential to also examine the initial conditions of cloud formation and early growth mechanisms in regions like the Dragon IDL.

Specifically, for the sphere ${\mathbb S}^{d-1} \subset {\mathbb R}^d$, the strict positive definiteness of a zonal function $f(\cos \theta)$ is governed by the signs of the coefficients in its expansion using Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$, where $\lambda=(d-2)/2$. While recent findings indicate that classical differentiation and integration preserve positive definiteness in this setting, these operations shift the space dimension in increments of two. This paper introduces operators for zonal functions on the sphere that maintain (strict) positive definiteness while transitioning between dimensions by steps of one. These fractional operators are specifically designed to act suitably on the Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$. Notably, this approach yields a new (strictly) positive definite function from a given one $\phi$ via the relation $\phi(\theta) = h(\theta)\psi_+ (\theta)$, where $h$ is a positive function and $\psi_+$ represents the even part of $\psi$, such that $\phi$ is Zonally Schur-Convex with respect to $\psi_+$. As the sphere admits an isometric embedding into a Hilbert space through (strictly) positive definite functions, this property allows us to order functions by geometric proximity. Notably, the even and odd parts of a zonal function on the sphere share this ordering when their coefficients relative to a single Gegenbauer polynomial are Zosmer-Convex. Furthermore, we establish similar results for Fourier series on the circle $\mathbb S^1$. Furthermore, for a zonally symmetric function $\phi$, its (strict) complete monotonicity in the angle $\theta$ is shown to be equivalent to the same properties holding for its kernel $k_\phi(x) = \phi(\arccos \langle x, y \rangle)$ in the argument $\langle x,y \rangle \in (-1,1)$. Finally, we provide examples demonstrating how these concepts facilitate the construction of Kriging matrices with all positive principal minors on the sphere. By integrating stress measurements with visual observations of various rough surfaces moving through dry liquid foams, we demonstrate the existence of three distinct friction regimes: slippage, stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. Our stress data aligns with established models for the slippage and anchored regimes, while we introduce a leverage rule to characterize stresses during stick-slip events. an elastic membrane dividing two fluids of differing densities under external pressure within a rotating Hele-Shaw cell. We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear primary finger states up to self-contact, as well as secondary branches involving mixed modes and circumferentially localized folds, varying with rotation rate and external pressure. The analysis includes both reflection-symmetric and symmetry-broken chiral configurations, with results illustrated through bifurcation diagrams. Furthermore, the ratio of the system scale to the natural length scale is identified as the key factor governing the sequence of primary bifurcations from the unperturbed circular state, as well as the resulting solution profiles and the initiation of secondary bifurcations. These findings offer insights into designing micro-mixing devices and provide a foundation for studying dynamic fingering patterns. A comparison is also made with previous studies on films under centrifugal acceleration exhibiting Rayleigh-Taylor instability. This work extends our prior publication found at https://doi.org/10.1093/jom/ufab018. Supplementary materials are available at https://doi.org/10.1093/jom/ozab048.

However, we observe that generating a target word relies not only on the source input but also heavily on previously generated target words, particularly distant ones that recurrent neural networks struggle to model effectively. To address this, we introduce a novel look-ahead attention mechanism designed to directly capture dependencies between target words. Additionally, we devise three integration patterns to incorporate this mechanism into conventional attention models. Experiments conducted on Chinese-to-English (NIST) and English-to-German (WMT) translation tasks demonstrate that our proposed look-ahead attention mechanism yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) generally employs sequence-to-sequence encoding and decoding, utilizing the context represented by compressed source semantics to generate translations word-by-word. While this approach effectively captures local dependencies within the source sentence, it often fails to model long-range dependencies between target words accurately. Although NMT has achieved state-of-the-art results, its error rate remains non-trivial, particularly when predicting words distant from the source input. This study presents a look-ahead attention mechanism that captures long-short term dependencies among target words by integrating future context (n+1-th target word) and past context (n-1-th target word), thereby enhancing the model's ability to handle long-range dependencies. Experiments on Chinese-to-English (NIST) and English-to-German (WMT) translation tasks show that our proposed method surpasses models using BSSE, NMT, and conventional attention mechanisms in term accuracy, overall BLEU score, and edit distance, with particular gains in words distant from the source utterance. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the English-German translation task and improves performance across all evaluation metrics on the Chinese-to-English task, confirming that look-ahead attention significantly boosts overall translation quality and accuracy, with a special emphasis on predicting words far removed from the source sentence. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/yzxir/Look-Ahead-Attention-for-NMT.

Abramson and Parashar contend that a comparable divide exists between sophisticated computational technologies and increasingly demanding applications, necessitating a parallel field known as translational computer science. Ultimately, this paradigm promotes a collaborative culture where researchers and engineers jointly pursue the goal of advancing computation-driven science. Utilizing low-energy effective field theories (EFTs) to model general neutrino interactions and Dirac fermion DM coupled to charm quarks, we conduct likelihood fits for individual neutrino and DM operators featuring distinct Lorentz structures and photon final-state radiation (FSR) parameters. We derive limits on neutrino EFT scales that are either complementary to or improve upon existing bounds from other invisible decay searches. Specifically, we introduce limits on DM EFT scales in regions previously unexplored by other experiments. By incorporating non-resonant background processes and accurately accounting for experimental acceptance and resolution, we demonstrate that future upgrades at the Jefferson Lab 12 GeV program could explore EFT scales up to several TeV for certain DM interactions. Furthermore, we provide an open-source framework of near- and post-resonance simulations and fits, enabling users to investigate various invisible decay final states and parametric configurations. The discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC has enabled physicists to probe whether the new physics it hints at manifests through deviations in precision electroweak observables or by directly detecting it at lower energy scales. This paper presents an effective field theory (EFT) analysis of Higgs-strangeness interactions, covering both tree-level and loop-level contributions. We examine multiple sources of electroweak precision data, including $Z$-pole measurements from LEP, the ATOMKI 1S to 2S electron capture data on protons, the muon anomalous magnetic moment ($g-2$), and various Higgs production and decay processes at the LHC. Since its introduction by Feller in the 1940s, parabolic arcs have been recognized as the typical trajectory of random walks conditioned to remain non-negative over a finite horizon. ### 1 Introduction

Lower gastrointestinal (GI) cancer, including colorectal and rectal cancers, represents a substantial global health burden. In the UK, it is the second most common cancer type after breast cancer, accounting for 11% of all new cases and 16% of cancer-related deaths in 2018 [1]. In the UK, large histology reports are generated weekly at six major hospital cancer centers. These reports are created by trained human pathologists who examine high-magnification cropped regions (approximately 2000 x 2000 pixels) derived from histology slides prepared from biopsy or resection samples. Although accurate reporting is vital for patient care, the current workflow is both time-consuming and labor-heavy. A single report may require analyzing up to 50 patches, with each patch taking roughly one minute to assess, resulting in approximately 5 hours of work per report. Consequently, there are currently fewer than 60 full-time pathologists available to serve six major cancer centers and one blood transfusion service across the UK [2]. This scarcity creates a risk of pathological backlog, forcing patients to endure delays in cancer diagnosis.

Although elastography can measure displacement both axially and laterally, axial estimates are superior due to higher sampling rates, resolution, and the propagation of the carrier signal along the axial axis. While Synthetic Aperture (SA) imaging offers better lateral resolution than other ultrasound techniques, its limited depth of field restricts its use in elastography. Virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) addresses this by applying synthetic aperture beamforming to focused transmitted data, thereby retaining SA's high lateral resolution while extending the depth of field. Furthermore, VSSA enhances lateral sampling frequency without the need for interpolation. This study employs VSSA for beamforming to achieve improved lateral resolution and sampling density, followed by processing with our recently introduced OVERWIND elastography technique [1]. Simulation and experimental outcomes demonstrate significant improvements in the accuracy of lateral displacement estimation. Ultrasound imaging provides a real-time view inside the human body, helping detect and monitor diseases such as cancer and guiding procedures like needle biopsies. Acoustic elastography evaluates the mechanical characteristics of biological tissues to support diagnosis and assess therapeutic success. Various imaging approaches exist for generating displacement maps, including conventional methods and speckle tracking. These methods rely on segmenting image regions based on similarity metrics like normalized cross-correlation (NCC), mutual information (MI), and normalized mutual information (NMI). These segmentation techniques divide the image into overlapping sub-blocks to estimate displacement, which are then combined to create displacement magnitude histograms. However, existing approaches often struggle with boundary accuracy, leading to inconsistencies in overlapping regions that require complex resolution processes. Our prior work [2] introduced the Optimal Value Region Watershed Network (OVRWN), which generates precise region boundaries using deep learning to improve bi-directional displacement estimation. This study further explores these findings with advanced synthetic aperture virtual source techniques.

By segmenting the grid into superstates, such as "rooms," the method establishes a dual-resolution decision-making system comprising local PEGs at the granular state level and an aggregated PEG at the superstate level. This paper examines a novel and potentially detrimental phenomenon where such overlap can hinder reinforcement learning. We introduce a theoretical framework analyzing multi-task training across overlapping task groups and identify a specific configuration of two overlapping sets that causes the agent to converge to a suboptimal solution, settling on a task-average policy rather than optimizing individual tasks. This adverse effect is not merely theoretical; we demonstrate through both a theoretical example and extensive experiments on a grid world that certain overlapping task sets can lead agents to learn a suboptimal task-average policy. These findings offer a theoretical foundation for understanding challenges in multi-task RL and provide a practical benchmark for evaluating and detecting risks in new multi-task learning frameworks. Ultimately, our work emphasizes the importance of carefully selecting task sets to avoid unwanted overlaps that may result in suboptimal outcomes. To address this issue, we propose three strategies for preventing task-average policy convergence and validate their effectiveness using a controlled two-task environment. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for practical multi-task reinforcement learning applications. Source code is available here: https://github.com/yzhou10/Task-Overlap.

These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques. By examining these proofs side-by-side, we can view Godel's Theorem as arising from a "representation" or "reflection" of formal arithmetic, resulting in a sentence that is neither provable nor refutable. Similarly, Tarski's Theorem can be seen as the representation/definability of truth in arithmetic, also yielding an undecidable sentence. Likewise, Godel-Carnap's Lemma yields a specific undecidable sentence regarding the non-provability or non-refutability of formulas. Finally, Rosser's Theorem shares this core structure but enhances it by introducing a priority ordering of formulas, again producing an undecidable sentence. We present these findings using a unified framework of representation and definition, which offers a streamlined approach to all four theorems. Notably, this perspective reveals a connection between representation/definability and recursion theory's "sweepout" theorems (or "parameter theorems"), allowing us to extend Godel-Carnap's Lemma and Rosser's Theorem even further. Our work builds upon previous studies by Smith (1980, 1985, 1989) and Pigiet (1982). The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/PJWolff/undecidability.

This paper presents an analysis of 34 years of Arecibo data regarding PSR B1133+16, yielding high-quality dynamic spectra and their corresponding scintillation arcs generated by screens along the line of sight. We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. While WN, a probabilistic autoregressive model utilizing stacked dilated convolutions, excels at high-fidelity audio synthesis, its reliance solely on data without prior audio knowledge hampers its ability to control pitch. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the most critical hyperparameters vary across different datasets and even between distinct models within the GCN family, validating the necessity of our solution. The source code for AutoGCN is openly available at https://github.com/zhengruipan/Graph_Convolutional_Network.

Upon implementing this condition via the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure, the resulting gauge-fixed action retains a dependence on a single gauge parameter. This indicates that the harmonic gauge represents a family of conditions rather than a unique one. This perspective provides a physical justification for covariant harmonic gauges, which arise when a mass term is introduced for the gravitational perturbation. Specifically, selecting a particular harmonic gauge yields a theory of linearized massive gravity with the expected five degrees of freedom, successfully avoiding the vDVZ discontinuity that plagues the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that appropriate gauge fixing within this framework offers a solution to the ambiguity regarding the divergence of the mass term in linearized massive gravity. An important consequence of this analysis is that the equivalence between harmonic gauge conditions relies on the spacetime being flat. When mass is present, these conditions are not equivalent, as the presence of mass introduces self-interactions that prevent the transformation between different gauges. In the weak mass limit, our findings reveal that the so-called zero-pole cancellation is not an intrinsic property of the theory but an artifact of using the harmonic gauge in curved spacetime. Finally, an appendix outlines the steps required to extend this approach to include gauge interactions.

Although GANs have proven effective in creating and altering natural images, their use within the medical field remains nascent. By leveraging the CheXpert dataset, we demonstrate that StyleGAN can be trained to produce authentic chest X-rays. Drawing inspiration from the Cyclic Reverse Generator (CRG) framework, we developed an encoder capable of accurately inverting the generator for synthetic X-rays and reconstructing real images at the organ level. Through guided manipulation of latent codes, we successfully imparted the condition of cardiomegaly (enlarged heart) to X-rays from healthy individuals. This research was featured at the Medical Imaging Meeting (MICCAI) Workshop on AI for Neglected Conditions in September 2020. The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/medic-lmu/StyleGAN_CheXpert. We invite researchers exploring AI-driven diagnosis and therapy to utilize our code, and we encourage the development of further innovations in this domain. Medical professionals worldwide are impacted by conditions that are difficult to diagnose or treat; addressing these challenges with AI could save countless lives. However, current AI research often concentrates on prevalent diseases like cancer and pneumonia, leaving many other conditions underserved. These neglected conditions may be underresearched because they are difficult to diagnose (as seen in retinal vein beading caused by diabetes) or hard to treat (such as cardiomegaly in chesterfield cats). This project employs style-based generative adversarial networks (StyleGAN) to perform realistic transformations on chest X-rays, specifically editing the cardiomegaly condition.
